state-to-state-purchases.story:
Countries have sold territory to each other for centuries. In these deals one state or ruler paid another for sovereignty, the legal right to rule the land. Scotland paid Norway 4,000 marks sterling for the Isle of Man and the Hebrides in 1266. The United States paid France $15 million for Louisiana in 1803, about $7 per square kilometre, and paid Russia $7.2 million for Alaska in 1867, about $4 per square kilometre.
The United States paid Denmark $25 million for the 400 square kilometres of the Danish West Indies in 1916, or $62,500 per square kilometre. As part of that deal it recognised Danish sovereignty over all of Greenland, a promise that came up again in later offers to buy the island. Brazil paid Bolivia £2 million for Acre in 1903. The last sale on the list is Gwadar, which Pakistan bought from Muscat and Oman for £3 million in 1958.
Every buyer and seller in Wikipedia's list of these sales is a state or a ruler, and no private buyer appears on it. The list leaves out leases and payments for other purposes such as war damages.
state-to-state-purchases.mechanism: A state can sell land to another state by treaty, and the buyer then has the right to rule it. Private buyers do not appear among the recorded sales.

greenland-purchase-offers.story:
The United States has tried several times to buy Greenland, the Arctic island that belongs to the Kingdom of Denmark and governs itself. Secretary of State William Seward backed a purchase in 1867, the same year the country bought Alaska, and there were talks again in 1910. In 1946 the United States secretly offered Denmark $100 million in gold, which Denmark rejected. In 2019 President Trump said he wanted to buy the island, and Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen called the idea absurd and said Greenland was not for sale.
In his second term from 2025 Trump pressed again and spoke of tariffs against Denmark. In January 2026 Greenland's leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen said Greenland would choose Denmark, and reports put opposition to an American takeover at 85 percent of Greenlanders. Under Greenland's Self-Government Act, independence is for the Greenlandic people to decide, followed by negotiation with Denmark and a referendum. On 22 September 2026 the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a security agreement in New York with no expiry date.
The agreement expands the American military presence and bars countries outside NATO, the Western military alliance, from setting up military installations. Frederiksen said it recognises Denmark's sovereignty, meaning its legal right to rule the island, and the Greenlandic people's right to decide their own future. No sale has taken place.
greenland-purchase-offers.mechanism: A state cannot be made to sell its territory, so a purchase needs the seller's agreement. In Greenland's case, the law also leaves the decision on independence to the people who live there.

romanov-empire-bakov.story:
The Romanov Empire is a self-declared country, or micronation, with no land of its own, started in 2011 by Anton Bakov, a Russian businessman and former member of the Russian parliament. He says it restores the Russian Empire. In 2014 it issued a manifesto naming the German prince Karl Emich of Leiningen as Emperor Nicholas III, and in 2017 it took the name Romanov Empire.
It sold passports online for 1,000 rubles, about $31, and claimed to have issued about 4,000 by 2014. To become a real state it needed territory, so Bakov talked with several countries about buying land. As of 2017, talks with Kiribati and the Gambia had failed. Nicholas III also wrote to Vladimir Putin asking for land in Yekaterinburg for a capital, and that request was denied.
In July 2013 Bakov said his state had granted citizenship to Edward Snowden, the former US intelligence contractor, who was then staying in Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow. In 2020 Bakov said a successor project called Arca Noë would be based on a floating settlement in neutral Mediterranean waters near Venice. It is not known to have been built.

white-rajahs-sarawak.story:
Sarawak, on the north-west coast of Borneo, was ruled for 105 years by a British family called Brooke. It had been a vassal territory of the Sultanate of Brunei, meaning it owed loyalty to the sultan. In 1841 Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II granted James Brooke, a man of British origin born in India, the area around the town of Sarawak (now Kuching) and the nearby Bau mining district, in return for help against piracy and uprisings.
Brooke was later confirmed with the title of Rajah. He rebuilt the government on the British model, and he and his successor leased or annexed more land from Brunei until the state covered much of northern Borneo. The title passed down the male line to a nephew and then to his son, Vyner Brooke. After the Japanese occupation in the Second World War, Vyner ceded Sarawak to the British Colonial Office in 1946.
Because it was unclear whether that cession, the formal handing-over of the territory, was legal, Britain also passed an annexation bill. His nephew and legal heir, Anthony Brooke, objected, and so did most native members of the Council Negri, the local parliament. A British governor, Duncan Stewart, was assassinated by members of a group seeking union with Indonesia. Sarawak became a British Crown colony and in 1963 a state of Malaysia.

british-north-borneo-company.story:
The British North Borneo Company was a private company that ran what is now Sabah, a state of Malaysia on the island of Borneo, for over 60 years. It began with a deal made by Baron von Overbeck, a German businessman and diplomat, and the brothers Alfred and Edward Dent, who headed a British trading firm in Shanghai and London. They wanted a colonial concession, meaning a grant of rights over the land.
In December 1877 the Sultan of Brunei agreed to one for 15,000 Spanish dollars. It then emerged that Brunei had already given some of the area to the Sultan of Sulu, so a second agreement was signed with him in January 1878 for 5,000 dollars a year. Overbeck and the Dents thereby became rulers of the territory. Overbeck left in 1879 after failing to interest Germany, and Alfred Dent turned to Britain, which granted the company a royal charter, its legal authority to operate, in November 1881.
The company issued laws, recruited police and set up courts. Britain made the territory a protectorate in 1888, meaning Britain took charge of its foreign relations. The Second World War left the company unable to pay for rebuilding, so in 1946 it handed North Borneo to the Colonial Office, the British government department for colonies, for £860,000 in cash. In 1949 an independent arbitrator, a person appointed to settle the dispute, awarded the company a further £1.4 million in compensation. The territory joined Malaysia in 1963.
british-north-borneo-company.why: Corrected: the 1878 Sulu payment was yearly, not a single sum (North Borneo dispute, Wikipedia; the same page's Sulu annual fee figure is consistent with the sulu-heirs entry). Cost field updated.

set.cost: 15,000 Spanish dollars to Brunei and 5,000 dollars a year to Sulu; Britain later paid £860,000 and an arbitrator awarded £1.4 million

sulu-heirs-arbitration.story:
This is a legal fight over the 1878 deal that handed part of northern Borneo, now the Malaysian state of Sabah, to the private British North Borneo Company. Under that deal the Sultan of Sulu either ceded or leased the land, a point never settled, and the company agreed to pay him and his heirs a yearly fee. Malaysia took over the payments after it was formed in 1963 and stopped them after the 2013 Lahad Datu standoff, an armed incursion into Sabah by followers of a Sulu claimant.
Eight people who say they are the sultan's heirs began arbitration in Spain in 2019. Arbitration is a private hearing where an appointed person decides a dispute in place of a court. Malaysia refused to take part, saying the matter belonged in its own courts. A Madrid court annulled the appointment of the arbitrator, Gonzalo Stampa, in 2021, so he moved the case to Paris and in February 2022 ordered Malaysia to pay $14.92 billion.
Spanish courts convicted Stampa of contempt of court, the offence of defying a court's order, and sentenced him to six months in prison. The conviction was upheld on appeal in May 2024. France's highest court ruled against the heirs in November 2024, and in December 2025 Malaysia announced that the Paris Court of Appeal had annulled the whole award because no valid arbitration agreement bound Malaysia. A spokesman for the sultanate said the legal fight was not over.
sulu-heirs-arbitration.mechanism: Heirs can try to use a contract from colonial times to claim money from the modern state that took over its payments. French courts held that the contract's dispute clause, which named a British consul-general whose post no longer exists, did not bind Malaysia to private arbitration.

rudd-concession.story:
The Rudd Concession was an 1888 agreement in which King Lobengula of Matabeleland, in what is now Zimbabwe, signed away the mineral rights of his kingdom to three men, Charles Rudd, Francis Thompson and Rochfort Maguire, who were agents of the businessman and politician Cecil Rhodes. Rhodes wanted to bring the region into the British Empire, and he needed the concession to win a charter for a company that could annex and govern it.
The text promised the king £100 every lunar month, 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles with 100,000 cartridges, and either a steamboat with guns on the Zambezi River or £500. In return the three men received complete and exclusive charge over all metals and minerals in his lands, and the power to do whatever they judged necessary to get them. The king also authorised them to keep out everyone else seeking land or mining rights, and agreed to grant no more concessions without their consent.
The document says this was because rival concession seekers had been bothering him. A witness named Helm certified that the terms had been explained to the king and his council. From 1889 Lobengula tried to disown the deal, saying that limits agreed orally had been left out, and sent envoys to Queen Victoria, without success. Britain granted a royal charter to Rhodes's British South Africa Company in October 1889, and the company occupied the neighbouring region of Mashonaland in 1890.
Its troops conquered Matabeleland in 1893 and 1894, and Lobengula died in exile soon afterwards. The company's charter ended in 1923, when Southern Rhodesia became a self-governing colony.
rudd-concession.mechanism: The written deal covered minerals only and gave no right to rule, but it became the legal basis for a royal charter that let a company annex and govern the country, meaning take it over as its own. The king's objections did not stop it.

cocos-clunies-ross.story:
The Cocos (Keeling) Islands are a small group in the Indian Ocean, now an Australian territory, that one Scottish family owned for about 150 years. The islands were empty until the 1820s, when an Englishman, Alexander Hare, arrived with a party made up mostly of people of Malay origin. Captain John Clunies-Ross, a Scottish seaman, settled in 1827 and began harvesting coconuts. Britain annexed the islands in 1857, and in 1886 Queen Victoria granted all the land to the Clunies-Ross family.
Sovereignty, the right to rule the islands, stayed with Britain, which ran them as a part of its Singapore colony, and in 1955 they became a territory of Australia. The family remained the landowner. In 1978 the Australian government paid A$6.25 million for the family's property, apart from their home, Oceania House, and its grounds on Home Island. In 1984 the Cocos Malay residents voted overwhelmingly to join Australia fully, in a United Nations-supervised vote called an Act of Self Determination. Australia bought the last of John Cecil Clunies-Ross's property in 1993 and sold Oceania House privately in 2001.
cocos-clunies-ross.mechanism: The family legally owned all the land under a grant from the Crown, while Britain and then Australia kept the right to rule the islands. So the Australian government got control of the land by buying it.

ruperts-land-sale.story:
Rupert's Land was a territory of 3.9 million square kilometres around Hudson Bay, about a third of present-day Canada, that a private company held for 200 years. King Charles II of England gave the Hudson's Bay Company a charter in 1670 with exclusive rights to trade and colonise all land whose rivers drained into the bay. The charter took no account of the sovereignty, or right to rule their own land, of the Cree, Assiniboine and other Indigenous peoples living there.
After Canada was formed in 1867, its government wanted the land, partly from fear that the United States, which had just bought Alaska, would take it. The company, for its part, lacked the money to govern a territory that was filling with settlers. It valued the land at up to $40 million, and the United States could have paid that, but Britain would not allow a sale to the Americans and pressed the company to deal with Canada.
After six months of talks the company agreed to £300,000, or about $1.5 million, and kept its trading posts and five per cent of the land, mostly prairie farmland. It signed the land over to the British Crown on 19 November 1869, and the Crown ceded it to Canada. The Red River Resistance, a rising by local people, delayed the transfer until 15 July 1870. Canada then negotiated seven treaties with Indigenous nations to obtain their consent to Crown sovereignty.

red-river-selkirk.story:
The Red River Colony was a settlement scheme around present-day Winnipeg in Canada, on a block of land the size of five Scotlands that a private company gave to one nobleman. Thomas Douglas, Earl of Selkirk, was troubled by the eviction of Scottish farmers in the Highland Clearances and believed emigration was their best hope. He saw that he needed one of the big fur companies on his side.
In 1811 the Hudson's Bay Company granted him 300,000 square kilometres out of its own territory, known as the Selkirk Concession or Assiniboia. The company expected the colony to grow food for its fur trade and cut the cost of shipping supplies. Selkirk bought many company shares in 1811 and 1812, and historians have debated how far that explains the grant. The rival North West Company opposed the colony, and the conflict turned violent.
In 1816 the colony's governor, Robert Semple, and about 20 settlers were killed at the Battle of Seven Oaks, and the settlement was abandoned for a time. Selkirk arrived the next year with about 100 disbanded soldiers and captured the rival's headquarters at Fort William. The land south of the 49th parallel passed to the United States under an 1818 treaty, and the colony existed until 1870, when the Hudson's Bay territory went to Canada.
red-river-selkirk.mechanism: A chartered company, one given its rights by the Crown, could pass part of its land to a private person. The grant gave him land under the company's charter and no independence from Britain.

palmyra-fullard-leo.story:
Palmyra is an uninhabited coral atoll in the central Pacific, 1,000 miles south of Hawaii, that was bought and sold by private owners while also being claimed by governments. The Kingdom of Hawaii annexed it in 1862 and two Hawaiian citizens became its joint owners. Their shares were then sold and inherited many times. In 1922 Henry Cooper sold his interest to Leslie and Ellen Fullard-Leo for $15,000, and they set up a company to harvest coconuts.
The atoll came under the United States when Hawaii did. The family tried from 1937 to lease it to the Navy, but during the talks the federal government sued them, claiming that the atoll had never been lawfully private property, and the Navy occupied it and built a runway during the Second World War. The US Supreme Court ruled for the Fullard-Leo and Cooper families in United States v. Fullard-Leo in 1947, which confirmed their private title against the government. The family later turned down offers to use the atoll as a nuclear waste dump or a casino, according to the Nature Conservancy, a conservation charity, which bought most of the land from them in 2000 for $30 million. Palmyra is now a federal wildlife refuge and the only incorporated US territory, meaning one treated as an integral part of the United States.
palmyra-fullard-leo.mechanism: Owning land and governing it are separate things. The family won clear private ownership against the federal government in court, and the atoll stayed under United States rule throughout.

herm-lease.story:
Herm is a tiny island in the Channel Islands, about a mile and a half long, part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a self-governing territory under the British Crown, whose right of use has been traded for over a century while the ownership stayed with a government. Prince Gebhard Blücher, a German noble, leased it from the British government in 1889 and brought in wallabies. The novelist Compton Mackenzie took over the tenancy in 1920.
The States of Guernsey, the island's government, bought Herm from the Crown in 1949 so that local people and tourists could enjoy it, and let it to Major Peter Wood, who restored the run-down island with his wife over 30 years. In 2008 his daughter and her husband put the remaining 40 years of their lease up for sale, asking £15 million. A trust called Starboard Settlement bought it for considerably less and formed Herm Island Ltd to run the island.
Talks on a 21-year extension broke down in 2013, with the tenant offering £440,000 and the States of Guernsey asking for £6 million. In 2023 the lease was extended to 2069 for an undisclosed sum, and Herm Island Ltd still runs the island.
herm-lease.why: Added from Wikipedia's Herm page: the lease was extended to 2069 in 2023, which the old story omitted. That page also gives 1946 as well as 1949 for the Guernsey purchase; 1949 kept.

franco-texian-bill.story:
The Franco-Texian Bill was a proposal in 1841 for the Republic of Texas, then an independent country, to grant three million acres to a private French company. Two Frenchmen, Basterrèche and de Lassaulx, wanted to set up the Franco Texian Commercial and Colonization Company. It was to bring in 8,000 families and build and keep up 20 forts for 20 years. In return it would receive the land, scattered along Texas rivers, and its settlers would pay no taxes or tariffs for 20 years.
It would also get exclusive trade with the New Mexico settlements and could develop mines, paying Texas 15 per cent of gross returns. The French envoy to Texas, Dubois de Saligny, and the Texas politician Sam Houston both supported it, and the Texas House of Representatives approved it on 23 January 1841. It never reached the Senate, because its sponsors saw they could not get the two-thirds majority needed to overcome a threatened veto by acting president David Burnet, so nothing was ever built.

poyais.story:
Poyais was a country that did not exist, sold to British investors and settlers in the 1820s by a Scottish adventurer named Gregor MacGregor. MacGregor had fought in the Venezuelan war of independence and briefly seized Amelia Island in Florida. In 1820 he persuaded the Mosquito King, an Indigenous ruler, to grant him about 8 million acres on the Caribbean coast of what is now Honduras.
The land was undeveloped jungle. Back in London he called himself the Cazique, or prince, of Poyais and described a prosperous nation with a capital and an opera house, backed by a guidebook, maps and documents that were nearly all fabricated. He sold a £200,000 bond and offered 100 acres of farmland for £11, along with military commissions and government posts. Two ships took about 250 settlers out in 1822 and 1823.
They found no capital or town, only undeveloped jungle, and malaria and other diseases spread among them until a ship from Belize rescued the survivors in May 1823. About two-thirds of the settlers died. MacGregor moved to Paris and tried again, was tried for fraud there and acquitted for lack of evidence, then sold more bonds and land certificates in London into the 1830s. He died in Venezuela in 1845 and was never convicted.

assab-rubattino.story:
Assab is a port in Eritrea on the Red Sea that started Italy's colony there through a private purchase. In the middle of the 19th century it was an Afar fishing village of about 100 people. On 15 November 1869 an Italian missionary, Giuseppe Sapeto, bought the bay on behalf of the Rubattino Shipping Company from two brothers, the sultans Hasan and Ibrahim ibn Ahmed, for 6,000 Maria Theresa thalers, a silver coin widely used in the region.
Sapeto argued that the port was well placed near the Bab-el-Mandeb strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, and that although it was nominally under the sultan of Aussa it was really independent. The press and parliament in Italy opposed the purchase, and Egypt declared the sale illegal. The Italian government took control of the port in 1882, and this led to the colony of Italian Eritrea.

singapore-1819-treaty.story:
The 1819 Singapore Treaty is the agreement that let a British trading company, the East India Company, set up in Singapore, and it is officially treated as the founding of the modern city. The company wanted a base to get around Dutch taxes on shipping in the region, and Stamford Raffles, a company official, won support in India to look for one. Signed on 6 February 1819, the treaty allowed the company to keep a factory, the old word for a trading post, in the lands of Sultan Hussein and Temenggong Abdul Rahman, the local chief.
In exchange the company would pay them 5,000 and 3,000 Spanish dollars a year. They also promised not to make a treaty with any other nation or let any other European or American power settle. Soon afterwards both men wrote to the Dutch and others saying they had been forced to sign. On 1 March Britain made them sign a statement of consent, and the Temenggong said his complaint had only been meant to head off Dutch retaliation. The British kept the post. In August 1824 a new treaty, drafted by the British official John Crawfurd, made the two rulers give up their full authority over Singapore and nearby islands in return for money allowances and the right to keep their property there.
singapore-1819-treaty.mechanism: The 1819 treaty paid yearly sums for the right to keep a trading post and to keep rivals out, and it did not hand over the right to rule. That came only with the second treaty in 1824.
singapore-1819-treaty.why: Story stopped in March 1819 with no outcome; added the 1824 treaty from the National Library Board page.

isle-of-man-revestment.story:
The Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea, was for a long time ruled under the Crown by a noble family, as its feudal lord, until the family sold those rights to the British government. A 1609 Act of Parliament had given the rights of Lord of Man to the Earl of Derby and his heirs, and they came down to the Dukes of Atholl. Because Parliament had fixed them by law, it took another Act to end them.
Under a contract with the British Treasury, Charlotte, Duchess of Atholl, sold the rights to the Crown for £70,000, and the Isle of Man Purchase Act of 1765, also called the Act of Revestment, put this into effect. Plans to merge the island into the English county of Cumberland met fierce local resistance, led by Sir George Moore, Speaker of the House of Keys, a chamber of the island's parliament, and did not go ahead.
The family kept its rights as local landlord, its power to choose the bishop and other privileges, and sold those in 1828 for £417,144.

transylvania-purchase.story:
The Transylvania Colony was an attempt by a North Carolina judge and land speculator, Richard Henderson, to create a private colony in what is now Kentucky and north central Tennessee. A 1763 British proclamation had forbidden colonial settlement west of the Appalachians, but Henderson's Transylvania Company hoped to get around this by buying the land directly from the Cherokee and winning approval as a British colony owned by its proprietors.
In 1775, at Sycamore Shoals, most leading Cherokee chiefs accepted a treaty selling the land for goods that some scholars estimate at about £10,000. Henderson hired Daniel Boone to cut the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap, and in May 1775 settlers agreed a written plan for a local government. Virginia and North Carolina both claimed parts of the same land. The Revolutionary War held back most settlement.
The Virginia legislature cancelled the claim in Kentucky in 1778, and North Carolina cancelled the Tennessee portion in 1783. Each compensated Henderson and his partners with a grant of 200,000 acres.
transylvania-purchase.mechanism: Buying from an Indigenous nation gave no ownership that colonial governments would accept. Virginia and North Carolina voided the claim because they claimed the same land, and paid Henderson off with smaller grants.

batmans-treaty.story:
Batman's Treaty was an 1835 attempt by British colonists to buy the land where Melbourne, Australia, now stands directly from its Aboriginal owners. It is the first and only documented time Europeans negotiated their presence directly with the traditional owners. The Port Phillip Association, a group of sheep farmers based mostly in Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania), wanted new pasture for sheep and sent John Batman across the strait with a deed drawn up by a lawyer.
On 6 June he met eight Wurundjeri and Boonwurrung elders. For 600,000 acres he handed over blankets, tomahawks, knives, scissors, looking glasses, handkerchiefs, shirts, clothes and flour, and the deed promised a yearly tribute. On 26 August the Governor of New South Wales, Richard Bourke, proclaimed such agreements void against the rights of the Crown and declared anyone on Crown land without authority a trespasser.
The Colonial Office in London approved this in October. Its objections were that Batman had bought from Aboriginal people, whom British colonists did not accept had any claim to land, and that he had bought for the Association instead of the Crown.

de-thierry-hokianga.story:
Charles de Thierry, the son of a French family who had fled to England, tried to create his own sovereign state in New Zealand before the Treaty of Waitangi of 1840. While at Cambridge he met Hongi Hika, a Ngāpuhi chief visiting England, and through the missionary Thomas Kendall arranged to buy 40,000 acres at Hokianga, in Northland, for 36 axes. In 1835 he reached the Pacific, announced himself King of Nuku Hiva in the Marquesas Islands, and wrote to the British government's representative in New Zealand that he would arrive as sovereign chief.
He recruited followers in Sydney in 1837, but on reaching Hokianga the chiefs Tāmati Wāka Nene and Patuone rejected his claims. They allowed him a plot of only 800 acres. His followers rioted and left, and he came to depend on Māori charity. The Treaty of Waitangi between the British Crown and Māori chiefs in 1840 ended any chance of his scheme. He moved to Auckland and taught piano until his death in 1864.
de-thierry-hokianga.mechanism: A purchase made at long distance through a go-between meant little once the local chiefs said it did not stand. Those chiefs could allow him to use land, but that gave him no right to rule it.

daewoo-madagascar.story:
In 2008 a South Korean company, Daewoo Logistics, agreed with the government of Madagascar to lease 1.3 million hectares of farmland for 99 years, an area larger than Qatar and by one report about half of the island's arable land. South Korea was one of the world's largest buyers of imported corn, and food prices had recently spiked, so Daewoo wanted to grow corn on 1 million hectares in the west and oil palm on 300,000 hectares in the east, for export.
It promised to spend $6 billion over 20 to 25 years on roads, railways, a port and schools. Critics said the deal ignored local people's customary use of the land, in a country where many could barely feed themselves. Anger over it helped fuel the movement against President Marc Ravalomanana, who had signed it, and he was driven from office in March 2009. Andry Rajoelina, the 34-year-old mayor of the capital, replaced him and within a day said the deal was off, because the constitution said Madagascar's land was neither for sale nor for rent.
A few months later a campaign group, Rainforest Rescue, said Daewoo still held 218,000 hectares. How that claim was resolved is not known.
daewoo-madagascar.mechanism: A lease gives a company the use of land while the state keeps the right to rule it. The new leader cancelled this one on the ground that the constitution barred selling or renting out land.

jarch-capital-south-sudan.story:
In January 2009 Philippe Heilberg, a former Wall Street banker who chaired the New York firm Jarch Capital, said he had secured leasehold rights, the right to use land for a fixed time, to 400,000 hectares in south Sudan, an area the size of Dubai. He did it by taking a majority stake in a company controlled by the son of Paulino Matip, a warlord who had fought on both sides of Sudan's civil war and became deputy commander of the southern army after a 2005 peace deal.
The Financial Times called it post-colonial Africa's biggest private land deal, second only to Daewoo's in Madagascar. Heilberg refused to say what he paid. He said he was betting that Sudan and possibly other African states would break apart, and that being in early on such shifts in sovereignty would pay off. Land law in the south was unclear, and experts and regional officials doubted he could enforce his rights. South Sudan did become independent in 2011. Whether the lease was ever enforced is not known.
jarch-capital-south-sudan.mechanism: A private investor bought rights from an armed commander instead of a government, hoping a future state would honour them. Such a deal gives no right to rule, and its value depends on who ends up in power.

greece-sell-islands-2010.story:
In March 2010, during Greece's debt crisis, two German members of parliament, Frank Schäffler of the pro-business Free Democrats and Marco Wanderwitz of Chancellor Angela Merkel's Christian Democrats, said the country should sell islands to raise cash. Greece's budget deficit had reached 12.7 per cent of its economy in 2009, against the European Union's limit of 3 per cent, and opinion polls showed Germans strongly against paying to rescue it. The newspaper Bild ran the story under the headline "Sell your islands, you bankrupt Greeks! And sell the Acropolis too!"
Schäffler said a country that needs to save money must sell its jewellery, so to speak, and privatise. Wanderwitz said Greece should give collateral for any European Union money it received, and that certain islands could serve. Greece's deputy foreign minister, Dimitris Droutsas, said such suggestions were not appropriate. The remarks named no buyer and no particular island.

tiran-sanafir.story:
Tiran and Sanafir are two Red Sea islands at the mouth of the Gulf of Aqaba, and Egypt agreed in April 2016 to hand them to Saudi Arabia. Tiran controls the shipping lane to the ports of Eilat in Israel and Aqaba in Jordan, and Egypt's closure of that lane helped cause the 1967 Arab-Israeli war. The Egyptian government says the islands were always Saudi and were put under Egypt's protection around 1950 because of tensions with Israel.
Critics link the transfer to billions of dollars of Saudi aid to the government of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi and call it a sell-off of national territory. The announcement, during a visit by the Saudi king, set off the largest protests against the government since 2014, and hundreds of people were arrested. The Supreme Administrative Court ruled against the transfer in January 2017, but another court set that ruling aside in April, and the Constitutional Court later halted all rulings in the case.
The head of parliament said it would not recognise any ruling on the agreement. On 14 June 2017, a day after police beat protesters in Cairo, parliament voted to approve it, and President Sisi ratified it on 24 June. A government report said the deal ended Egypt's sovereignty, its right to rule the islands, while Egypt kept administering them for the time being.
tiran-sanafir.mechanism: The right to rule the islands was to pass by treaty between two states. The Egyptian government calls it the return of Saudi islands and critics call it a sale, and an Egyptian court and parliament came to opposite conclusions.

tompkins-patagonia.story:
Douglas Tompkins, the American who founded the clothing firms The North Face and Esprit, spent about three decades buying more than a million hectares of Chile and Argentina to create private nature reserves. He moved to southern Chile after leaving business in 1990 and used go-betweens to buy parcels in Chaitén province, to avoid attention and rising prices. In 1994 he announced Pumalín Park, 275,000 hectares running from the Pacific Ocean to the Argentine border, which in effect cut Chile in two.
Chile had recently come out of dictatorship and had nearly gone to war with Argentina over this frontier, so parliament debated whether he was undermining national sovereignty. The military and Patagonian senators objected, and small farmers without land titles said he ignored their rights. In 1996 he agreed with President Frei to stop buying land and to allow infrastructure across it. That agreement was later cancelled by both sides, and he more than doubled his Chilean holdings and bought more in Argentina.
He promised to give all the land to the state, but distrust between him and the government had limited his donations when he died in a kayaking accident in December 2015. His widow, Kristine McDivitt Tompkins, pledged more than one million acres to Chile in March 2017, and in January 2018 President Michelle Bachelet announced decrees creating national parks from it, including Pumalín and Patagonia.
tompkins-patagonia.mechanism: Tompkins bought private ownership of the land while Chile and Argentina kept the right to rule it. Chile's politicians still treated one foreign owner's control of a strip from the coast to the border as a question of national territory.
tompkins-patagonia.why: Story ended at his death in 2015 and missed the outcome, the 2017-18 donation to Chile. Added from the retrieved page. status is still 'operating'; caller may prefer 'absorbed' for the donated Chilean land.

add_sources.t: Chile has created 5 national parks from donated land, World Economic Forum, Feb 2018

benetton-patagonia.story:
The Italian clothing group Benetton is the largest private landowner in Argentina, holding about 970,000 hectares in Patagonia since it bought the Compañía de Tierras Sud Argentino in 1991. That company dates from 1889, when the Argentine government gave land to 10 British citizens, 90,000 hectares each, passing over the Mapuche people who lived there, many of whom ended up as labourers on the new ranches.
In 2002 a Mapuche couple, Atilio Curiñanco and Rosa Nahuelquir, moved with their children onto Santa Rosa, a 534-hectare part of the Leleque ranch, believing it was government land. The company complained, and police removed them and destroyed their home and crops. A judge cleared them of criminal blame, but ruled in the civil case that the land was Benetton's. In 2004 they travelled to Rome with the Nobel Peace laureate Adolfo Pérez Esquivel to meet Luciano Benetton, who promised to look for a solution.
He offered the Chubut provincial government 7,500 hectares elsewhere for Mapuche farming, and the province rejected it as unproductive. In February 2007, 25 Mapuche including six families occupied Santa Rosa again, saying it was their ancestral territory. In March 2011 Judge Omar Magallanes ruled for Benetton, gave the company the disputed land and ordered the residents to leave within 10 days. The community appealed, and how that appeal ended is not known.
benetton-patagonia.mechanism: The purchase gave the company legal ownership under Argentine law, and that ownership traces to an 1889 state grant made without the consent of the Mapuche. Argentina kept the right to rule the land, and its courts have treated the company's ownership as valid.
benetton-patagonia.why: Old story said the end of the 2007 occupation was unreported, but a March 2011 ruling is reported on the retrieved page. That page dates the reoccupation to 2008 and IPS to February 2007; February 2007 kept.

add_sources.t: Argentina: Mapuche win one, lose one in land disputes, CounterVortex

trump-gaza.story:
On 9 February 2025, President Donald Trump told reporters on Air Force One, "I'm committed to buying and owning Gaza," referring to the Palestinian coastal territory devastated by war. He said other Middle Eastern states might rebuild sections under American auspices and that the United States would make sure Hamas, the Palestinian armed group that had ruled Gaza, did not move back. He had also spoken of permanently moving Palestinians out to create a "Riviera of the Middle East".
His remarks named no seller and no price. Ezzat El Rashq of the Hamas political bureau answered that "Gaza is not a property to be sold and bought" and said Palestinians would defeat any displacement plans.
trump-gaza.mechanism: A purchase needs a seller with the power to hand over the land. The statement named none, and Hamas rejected the idea of a sale.

huang-nubo-grimsstadir.story:
In 2011 Huang Nubo, a Chinese businessman who founded the property firm Zhongkun Group, tried to buy about 300 square kilometres of wilderness at Grímsstaðir á Fjöllum in north-eastern Iceland, equal to 0.3 per cent of the country. He offered about $10 million for the land, which was partly owned by the government, and planned to spend about $200 million on a tourist resort and a nature reserve.
Icelandic law bars large land purchases by people or companies from outside the European Economic Area, a group of European countries that share a single market, so he needed an exemption. Interior Minister Ögmundur Jónasson refused in late 2011. He said an exemption would make the law meaningless and could encourage others to buy up large parts of Iceland. The Social Democrats leaned toward the deal and the minister's Left Greens opposed it, and one Social Democrat member of parliament called the decision crazy.
Huang called the minister a racist. In May 2012 a committee of three ministries recommended a smaller deal, a 40-year lease of two to three square kilometres for a hotel and tourist facilities. Huang had said that building one hotel did not interest him. The lease is not known to have been signed.
huang-nubo-grimsstadir.mechanism: A country can limit who may buy its land by nationality, and here a minister refused to waive that limit. The bid concerned land ownership only, and the right to rule the land was never on offer.

nile-trading-mukaya.story:
Nile Trading & Development is a Texas company that in March 2008 signed a 49-year lease over about 600,000 hectares in Mukaya Payam, a district of Lainya County in what is now South Sudan, for $25,000. According to the Oakland Institute, a California research group that published the contract, the lease gave unrestricted rights to exploit all natural resources on the land, with the possibility of nearly a million acres more.
After the Institute's report spread in 2011, the year South Sudan became independent, local people mobilised against it. Chiefs and county authorities protested in July, and in August a committee of chiefs, state legislators and officials went to the capital, Juba, to reject the lease before President Salva Kiir. Kiir replied that the matter should be settled according to their will. The Institute announced that the deal had been effectively stalled. Whether it was ever formally cancelled is not known.
nile-trading-mukaya.mechanism: A lease signed before South Sudan's independence gave a foreign firm wide rights for a small price. It gave the firm no right to rule, and local opposition reached the president.

sark-fief-sales.story:
Sark, one of the Channel Islands, is a fief, land held from the British monarch, and with the Crown's permission its lordship may be mortgaged or sold. It has changed hands this way. In the 1730s a widow, Susanne le Pelley, bought it. In 1844 the Seigneur, or lord, Ernest le Pelley, needed money to keep a silver mine running and got Crown permission to mortgage the fief for £4,000 to John Allaire, a Guernsey privateer, or licensed ship raider, reputed to be the richest man in Guernsey.
Allaire died within two years and his daughter Marie Collings took over the mortgage. The mine closed in 1847 after its deepest gallery collapsed, and the next Seigneur, Pierre Carey le Pelley, could not keep up the payments. When she moved to take the island for the unpaid loan, he asked Queen Victoria's permission to sell, and in December 1852 Collings bought the lordship for £6,000 less the loan and interest, which left £1,383 to pay.
She never visited and died the next year. Her family still holds the title. Sark's parliament became fully elected in 2008.

hospitaller-caribbean-1651.story:
From 1651 to 1665 the Knights of Malta, a Catholic military order, owned four Caribbean islands: Saint Christopher (now Saint Kitts), Saint Croix, Saint Barthélemy and Saint Martin. They came to the order through Phillippe de Poincy, a knight who was also France's governor there and who had defied the French company that ran the islands, driving off the replacement it sent. To keep his post he suggested in 1649 that the order buy them.
The Company of the American Islands was failing and it dissolved in 1651, selling its rights. Under a treaty with France two years later the king kept the final right to rule, while the knights had full civil and religious authority, could send only French knights as governors, and owed a gold crown worth 1,000 écus to each new king. Poincy ruled as he liked until his death in 1660 and built forts and a grand residence.
A rebellion overthrew the order's rule on Saint Croix in 1657 and Caribs attacked Saint Barthélemy. The colonies made no profit and the order still owed France part of the purchase price. Under pressure from the French minister Colbert it sold them in 1665 to the new French West India Company.
hospitaller-caribbean-1651.mechanism: A religious order bought islands from a bankrupt company. It held ownership and full local government, while the French king kept the final right to rule.

du-parquet-islands.story:
Jacques Dyel du Parquet was a French soldier and the governor of Martinique, who in 1650 bought Martinique, Grenada, Saint Lucia and the Grenadines in the Caribbean from the company he served. The Company of the American Islands was collapsing and selling off its rights. The contract was signed in Paris on 27 September 1650, with the king's approval following in August 1651, and the king made du Parquet governor over the islands he now owned.
Wikipedia's article on him gives the price as 41,500 livres paid in instalments, while its article on the company gives 60,000 livres. He had already founded settlements on Grenada and Saint Lucia. On Grenada his settlers fought the indigenous islanders from 1649 until the last resistance was crushed in 1654. He sold Grenada in 1655 to Jean Faudoas, Count of Serillac. On his death in 1658 the king appointed his young son governor of Martinique and Saint Lucia.
In April 1664 the king revoked all the sales the company had made to private buyers, and a new French West India Company was set up that May.
du-parquet-islands.mechanism: A private buyer acquired islands and then received the governorship from the king, who kept the final right to rule. The king later cancelled such sales by decree, so ownership lasted only while the Crown allowed it.

lanai-ellison.story:
Lānaʻi is the sixth-largest Hawaiian island, 364 square kilometres, and 98 per cent of it belongs to Larry Ellison, co-founder of the software firm Oracle. He bought that share in June 2012 for $300 million. The other 2 per cent, including the harbour and the homes of about 3,400 residents, belongs to the state or to homeowners. Single owners have held most of the island for over a century.
Walter Gibson bought land there for $3,000 in 1863 with Mormon church money, titled it in his own name and was excommunicated, and by the 1870s he held most of the island. By 1907 the rancher Charles Gay owned about half. A law barred the government from selling him so much land, so he got the rest by swapping some Honolulu land for it. James Dole bought the island in 1922 and made it the world's largest pineapple plantation, and it passed to David Murdock in 1985 when he bought the parent company. Ellison has spent an estimated $450 million remodelling the island's Four Seasons resort, which reopened in 2016.

casado-chaco.story:
The Carlos Casado company, set up in Rosario, Argentina, bought huge areas of the Chaco, the dry forest region of western Paraguay, when the Paraguayan state sold public land in the late 19th century. It acquired over 7,800 square kilometres in 1886 and came to hold more than 5 million hectares. It cut quebracho trees to make tannin, a substance used for tanning hides, and built the town of Puerto Casado, founded in 1889, and a railway running about 150 kilometres west from the Paraguay River.
Mennonite settlers passed through from 1926, and in the Chaco War the port served as a military post and the railway carried soldiers, supplies and wounded. The company stopped production in the late 1990s and its tannin factory is shut. It also sold its land, including the town, to a group called the Moon Sect, after the Korean religious leader Sun Myung Moon, and local residents, among them Guaraní people, marched nearly 600 kilometres to Asunción to ask the government to expropriate it, meaning take it over for public use.
casado-chaco.mechanism: A state sold public land to a company on a very large scale. The company owned the land and Paraguay kept the right to rule it, though the company's town and railway served the region.
casado-chaco.why: Railway length corrected to about 150 km per Wikipedia's Puerto Casado page. Thin ending filled from the same page.

swazi-concessions.story:
During the reign of King Mbandzeni of Swaziland, now Eswatini, which lasted until 1889, white settlers from Britain and the Transvaal, the Boer republic next door, obtained a mass of concessions, grants of rights over land, mining, trade and even administration. Concession seekers crowded his capital at Mbekelweni, and interest grew after gold was found in the Transvaal. He and his officials granted many overlapping rights and were paid in gold, cattle or goods, with advice from 'Offy' Shepstone, a nephew of the Natal colonial official Theophilus Shepstone.
By one account, Boers tricked the king, who could not read or write, into marking papers with a cross after telling him the land concessions were not permanent, though the papers said they were. These concessions led to treaties between outside powers in 1884 and 1894 that reduced Swaziland's borders and made it a protectorate of the South African Republic, meaning that state took charge of its outside affairs. Mbandzeni is quoted as saying on his deathbed that the Swazi kingship would die with him.

firestone-liberia.story:
In 1926 the American tyre maker Firestone won a 99-year lease on up to a million acres of Liberia, in West Africa, at six cents an acre, wherever in the country it chose. That was 4 per cent of Liberia's territory and nearly 10 per cent of its land then considered arable. Harvey Firestone wanted American-grown rubber because a British scheme had pushed up prices, and Liberia's government wanted American protection from colonial neighbours eager to annex it.
After the legislature approved a draft, Firestone added a clause requiring Liberia to take a $5 million loan from his own company, at 7 per cent. The money was meant to pay off debts to British banks, and Liberia agreed under pressure from the US State Department. An American financial adviser then controlled Liberia's budget, and the country could not borrow without the company's consent.
The company was largely exempted from taxes and displaced local residents. By 1932 the loan took nearly all government revenue. When Liberia missed a payment, Firestone asked the US government to send a warship, and President Roosevelt refused. The company still runs the world's largest contiguous rubber farm, at Harbel.
firestone-liberia.mechanism: Liberia remained independent, but a lease and a loan together gave a company land and a say over state finances. One account calls the result an American protectorate in practice, meaning a country controlled by a stronger one, though Liberia kept its formal right to rule itself.

sazan-kushner.story:
Sazan is an uninhabited island off Albania's Adriatic coast, once a Soviet submarine base, and Zvërnec is the strip of beach and lagoon opposite it. Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, the son-in-law and daughter of US President Donald Trump, plan a luxury resort there. In 2026 Ivanka Trump said the couple owns about five miles of beachfront opposite the island. Albania's government has given preliminary approval.
The coast lies in the protected Vjosa-Narta area, home to about 250 bird species. In 2024 Prime Minister Edi Rama's government passed a law that removed the area's protected status and allowed five-star hotels, and environmental groups have gone to court, arguing that it breaks Albanian and European Union law. In June 2026 thousands protested in Tirana for days, with some saying the government was selling land that was not its to sell.
That month prosecutors froze the accounts of a firm owned by the Qatari brothers Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat, who are helping finance the project, in an inquiry into fraudulent land titles. A representative said Kushner's Affinity Partners has no role and that partners invest personally. The investigative journalist Lindita Cela traced the land's ownership through a chain of shell companies, firms with no real business of their own, running from Albania to the Netherlands.
sazan-kushner.mechanism: A government can open protected public land to private developers by changing its law. Albania keeps the right to rule the land, and the dispute is over who had the right to give it away.
sazan-kushner.why: Corrected per KPBS/NPR: Trump said they own the beachfront opposite the island, not both the island and the strip. The law also removed protected status. status is 'operating' although the resort has only preliminary approval, and caller may want to review that.

puertopia-sol.story:
Puertopia, later renamed Sol, was a plan by wealthy cryptocurrency investors to build a new city in Puerto Rico, a US territory, in which the money would be virtual and contracts public. They arrived after Hurricane Maria in September 2017, drawn by tax rules that spare residents federal income tax and capital gains tax. Their leader was Brock Pierce, director of the Bitcoin Foundation and co-founder of the blockchain firm Block.One.
In early 2018 they toured properties and debated buying the Roosevelt Roads Naval Station, 9,000 acres with two deep-water ports. Another resident said they had told him they would buy 250,000 acres and incorporate their own city. Some members thought moving into Old San Juan was enough. A local critic spoke of crypto colonialism, and another Puerto Rican called the island a tax playground for the rich. They are not known to have bought the base or founded a city.

sealand.story:
Sealand is a former British sea fort in the North Sea whose occupants have claimed since 1967 that it is an independent country. The fort, Roughs Tower, was built during the Second World War about 6 nautical miles off Suffolk and 7 off Essex, then outside Britain's three-mile territorial sea, the coastal belt a state fully controls. Roy Bates, a former army major, had just been convicted for running a pirate radio station on a fort inside the limit.
He moved to Roughs Tower at the end of 1966, took it from Radio Caroline staff, and declared the Principality of Sealand on 2 September 1967. In May 1968 his son Michael fired a pistol near a boat servicing a navigation buoy, and both were taken to court. A judge at Chelmsford ruled that October that the firearms law did not apply, because Parliament had never extended it beyond the three-mile limit.
In 1978 a court in Cologne refused a request by Alexander Achenbach, a German who called himself its prime minister, to drop his German citizenship, holding that Sealand was no state. That August Achenbach's lawyer Gernot Pütz seized the platform. The Bateses retook it by helicopter and fined Pütz 75,000 Deutsche Marks. In 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, which now covers the tower.
A fire in 2006 sent one person to hospital, and a 2007 attempt by The Pirate Bay file-sharing site to buy the fort failed. Roy Bates died in 2012. His son Michael now lives in England, and the family sells noble titles and an online citizenship costing about $10 a month, while one caretaker lives on the fort.

rose-island.story:
The Republic of Rose Island was a platform in the Adriatic Sea, nearly 12 kilometres off Rimini, Italy, whose builder declared it an independent country. Giorgio Rosa, an engineer from Bologna who enjoyed engineering experiments and disliked property bureaucracy, conceived it in 1958 and placed it a few hundred metres outside Italian territorial waters, the coastal belt a state fully controls. It was a 400-square-metre deck on nine pylons.
Late in 1966 the Rimini harbour office asked him to stop work, partly because nearby areas were leased to the state energy company ENI. He carried on and opened to visitors in summer 1967, with a bar, restaurant, nightclub, shop and post office. On 1 May 1968 he declared independence, with himself as president and Esperanto as the language. Italian officials suspected the project was a way to avoid tax on tourist income.
On 26 June police and tax officers took control and blockaded the platform, with only a guard and his partner aboard. Rosa telegraphed Italy's president, Giuseppe Saragat, and got no reply. In August the merchant marine ministry ordered demolition, and his appeal failed. The platform survived two explosive charges in February 1969, and a storm sank it on 26 February. The Council of State, Italy's top administrative court, then held the claims of independence unfounded and said Italian citizens stay subject to Italian law abroad. A 2020 Netflix film, Rose Island, tells the story.

xlii-seastead-phuket.story:
XLII was a small floating home placed in the Andaman Sea about 14 nautical miles off Phuket, Thailand. A seastead is a permanent home at sea, and its backers hope to live under no country's laws. This one was a six-metre-wide cabin raised on a weighted column, paid for and built by a company called Ocean Builders. Chad Elwartowski, a 46-year-old American bitcoin trader, and his Thai partner Supranee Thepdet moved in during early 2019.
Elwartowski said 20 more would be sold to form a community. The Thai navy said they had announced autonomy beyond the reach of any court and invited others to join, and Thailand treated this as an attack on its sovereignty, its right to rule its own territory. The couple left before the navy raided the cabin on 13 April 2019. Thailand revoked Elwartowski's visa and charged the two under a law that carries life in prison or death.
On 22 April navy boats began towing the cabin to shore as evidence. Ocean Builders said it sat in the contiguous zone, the band 12 to 24 miles out where a country has only limited powers, and that no micronation was intended. Thailand pointed to its 200-mile exclusive economic zone, where a coastal state controls resources. In June 2019 officials said there had been no progress in arresting the couple, who had been traced to Tarutao island in April. In July prosecutors said nine more suspects would be charged. How the case ended is not known.

bir-tawil-kingdom-of-north-sudan.story:
Bir Tawil is a stretch of 2,060 square kilometres of desert on the border between Egypt and Sudan that neither country claims, and in 2014 an American farmer declared it a kingdom. This status comes from two lines the British drew when they controlled the region. In 1899 they drew a straight border along the 22nd parallel. In 1902 they drew an administrative line that followed how local tribes used the land.
Egypt relies on the first line and Sudan on the second, because each line gives that country the larger Hala'ib Triangle. Under either country's position, Bir Tawil belongs to the other, so nobody claims it. On 16 June 2014 Jeremiah Heaton, a farmer from Virginia, planted a blue flag there and declared the Kingdom of North Sudan so that his daughter could be a princess. It was her seventh birthday.
He said he asked for permission in Cairo to make the trip. He later applied for observer status at the United Nations, offered honorary titles for $25 and offered the right to name a capital city for $1.75 million. Noam Leshem, a geographer at Durham University, told Al Jazeera that the land's status is ambiguous and that tribes still use it. No government has recognised the kingdom, meaning none has accepted it as a state, and no one has settled there.
bir-tawil-kingdom-of-north-sudan.mechanism: This case tests whether a private person can acquire land that no government claims. International law allows only states to take terra nullius (land belonging to no state), so Heaton's flag and website gave him no legal ownership.

prospera-zede.story:
Próspera is a private business zone with its own rules on Roatán, an island off the north coast of Honduras. In 2013 Honduras changed its constitution to allow Zones for Employment and Economic Development (ZEDEs), areas with their own laws, courts and taxes. An earlier plan called Special Development Regions had been struck down as a breach of sovereignty, the country's right to govern itself.
Erick Brimen, a Venezuelan-born fund manager, applied in 2017 and built Próspera with American venture capital, through a Delaware company that holds a veto on its council. It offers single-digit taxes, its own regulations and a court of retired Arizona judges who hear cases online. Neighbours in the village of Crawfish Rock feared losing their land. President Xiomara Castro signed a repeal of the ZEDE law in April 2022, saying Honduras was recovering its sovereignty.
On 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court declared the ZEDE laws unconstitutional, with retroactive effect. Próspera's owners had already claimed about $10.8 billion from Honduras at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), a World Bank body that decides disputes between investors and governments. They relied on a promise of stable rules and on CAFTA-DR, a trade treaty between the United States and Central American countries.
Honduras left ICSID in August 2024, then rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026. Honduran officials said in October 2025 that the claim had dropped to $1.63 billion. The case was still pending in October 2026, when the tribunal issued an order about a site visit, and the zone continues to operate during the dispute.
prospera-zede.why: Story said $10.7 billion and the cost field $10.8 billion. Revista E&N gives US$10,775 million, so story aligned at $10.8 billion.

somaliland.story:
Somaliland is a self-declared state in the Horn of Africa, on the Gulf of Aden, which has governed itself since 1991 while Somalia still claims it as its own. It covers 176,120 square kilometres and has about 6.2 million people. It was a British protectorate that united with Somalia in 1960, but the constitution put to a referendum in 1961 had little support in the north.
Harsh policies against the Isaaq clan under Somalia's president Siad Barre led to a 10-year war, and it ended with a declaration of independence in 1991 as Somalia fell into civil war. Since then Somaliland has held its own elections, run its own government and issued its own currency, the Somaliland shilling. The New York Times reported that it has governed most of the land it claims largely in peace and stability.
For decades no country recognised it, meaning accepted it as a state. It kept informal ties and hosted offices from Ethiopia and Taiwan. On 26 December 2025 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu signed an agreement recognising it as an independent and sovereign state, making Israel the first UN member to do so. As of October 2026 Israel remained the only one. According to The New York Times, other governments fear recognition could encourage secession elsewhere.

asgardia.story:
Asgardia is a self-declared space nation run from Vienna, Austria, whose only territory has been one small satellite. The Russian engineer Igor Ashurbeyli announced it at a press conference in Paris on 12 October 2016. People could join online, and over 100,000 applied within two days and 500,000 within three weeks, though tougher checks cut the figure to about 210,000 by June 2017. A constitution passed that month, with no formal way to vote against it, and made the state a kingdom.
On 12 November 2017 an Antares rocket from Virginia carried the satellite Asgardia-1, weighing 2.8 kilograms, into orbit, and Asgardia called itself the first nation with all its territory in space. Legal scholars disagreed, because US companies launched the satellite on a NASA-funded mission and it stayed under US authority. The Outer Space Treaty bars countries from claiming space and holds the launching state responsible for what it launches.
Its parliament met in Vienna, and Ashurbeyli was inaugurated as head of nation at the Hofburg palace on 25 June 2018 and re-elected with 93.17 percent in September 2022. The satellite burned up in the atmosphere on 12 September 2022, and no replacement has been reported. A press release from Asgardia reports a congress in Dubai on 30 October 2025 and claims over one million citizens. No state or UN body recognises it, and no one has ever lived there.

lunar-embassy.story:
Lunar Embassy is a company that sells deeds to land on the Moon and other planets, run by Dennis Hope, an entrepreneur in Nevada. In 1980, going through a divorce and short of money, Hope read the Outer Space Treaty in a library. Article II bars nations from taking land in space, and Hope concluded that this left individuals free to do so. He filed a claim to the Moon, the other planets and their moons, and sent it to the United Nations with a note saying he meant to subdivide and sell it, asking them to tell him of any legal problem.
Hope says they never replied, and he treats that silence as approval. He began selling full time in 1995. Discover magazine reported $9 million in sales to 4.25 million people at $19.99 a sale, and in a Vice interview he claimed 611 million lunar acres sold, plus plots on Mars, Venus, Io and Mercury. In 2001 customers asked about their rights, so he wrote a constitution for a Galactic Government, which he says was ratified online in March 2004 by 173,562 votes.
Ram Jakhu, a space law professor at McGill University, says the treaty was written to block such claims and no one can own property in outer space. No government has ruled on the deeds, and the company's website was still selling them in 2026.
lunar-embassy.mechanism: The UN's failure to reply gave Hope no ownership. Legal experts read the Outer Space Treaty's ban as blocking private claims along with national ones.
lunar-embassy.why: Corrected: Discover (2007) gives $19.99 per sale, with no price per acre.

south-sudan-2011.story:
South Sudan, in east-central Africa, became an independent country on 9 July 2011 after voting to leave Sudan. The vote came from the 2005 Naivasha Agreement, also called the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, between the central government in Khartoum and the Sudan People's Liberation Army/Movement, the southern rebel movement. It ended the long war between north and south and fixed the terms and date of a referendum in advance.
For the result to count, turnout had to reach 60%, and a simple majority would then mean separation. The vote first needed a census, which was delayed three times, and voter registration. Both were hard to carry out because of unmapped minefields in the south, up to 5 million nomadic Sudanese, and up to 2 million displaced southerners in camps around Khartoum. Voting ran from 9 to 15 January 2011. Final results, published on 7 February, showed 98.83% for separation on a turnout of 97.58%.
Ballots were suspended in 10 of 79 counties because turnout there came to more than 100%, and the result was still well above the 60% turnout needed. A parallel vote on whether Abyei, a disputed border area, would join the south was postponed over arguments about borders and who could vote, and it has been put off indefinitely. South Sudan joined the UN on 14 July 2011.
south-sudan-2011.mechanism: When the parent state agrees in a peace deal to a vote on separation, with the date fixed in advance, the result is likely to be accepted. Sudan had agreed to the vote and accepted the outcome, so South Sudan was quickly admitted to the UN.

kosovo-2008.story:
Kosovo is a territory in the Balkans, in south-eastern Europe, that declared independence from Serbia in 2008 and is recognised by more than half of UN members. It had been an autonomous province, one with its own local government, within Serbia, which was then part of Yugoslavia. In 1990 its assembly voted to declare independence, and only Albania recognised that. After the Kosovo War, UN Security Council Resolution 1244 placed it under a UN mission from 1999, with a NATO-led force providing security.
As control passed to the UN, an estimated 100,000 Serbs and other non-Albanians fled. On 17 February 2008, 109 of the 120 assembly members adopted a new declaration of independence. Serbia called it illegal and that year persuaded the UN General Assembly, by 77 votes to 6 with 74 abstentions, to ask the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, for an opinion. On 22 July 2010 the court ruled 10 to 4 that the declaration did not violate international law.
Later talks led to a deal between the governments of Serbia and Kosovo, signed in Brussels in 2013. Kosovo is recognised by 110 UN members, Taiwan, the Cook Islands and Niue, and 8 other UN members have withdrawn recognition. It belongs to the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, but it is not a UN member.

order-of-malta.story:
The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is a Catholic religious order that has no land but is treated as a sovereign body, like a state, in international law. It began in the 11th century as a hospital community in Jerusalem, and Pope Paschal II approved it in 1113. It later ruled the island of Rhodes and then Malta, which it defended for more than three months against the Ottoman Empire in the Great Siege of 1565.
In June 1798 Napoleon's forces took Malta and the Order lost its last territory. Other countries went on treating it as a sovereign body. Its only property of this kind is two headquarters buildings in Rome with extraterritorial status, meaning Italian law treats them as outside normal Italian control. It issues its own passports, coins and stamps, and signs treaties. Its website reports diplomatic relations with 118 countries and the European Union, while Wikipedia gives 115 states.
The United Nations General Assembly made it a permanent observer in 1994, citing its humanitarian work. Only three of its senior officers count as its citizens. It says its diplomatic network exists to give its medical programmes protected access in crisis regions.

wonga-coup-equatorial-guinea.story:
The Wonga Coup was a failed 2004 plot by foreign mercenaries, soldiers for hire, to overthrow Teodoro Obiang, president of the oil-rich African country of Equatorial Guinea, and replace him with the exiled politician Severo Moto. It was organised by mainly British financiers. Prosecutors said Moto offered the group $1.8 million and oil rights. On 7 March 2004 police at Harare airport in Zimbabwe impounded a Boeing 727 from South Africa carrying three crew and 64 former soldiers.
They arrested the former British special forces officer Simon Mann by the runway as he waited for arms to be loaded. Mann said the weapons were for guarding diamond mines in Congo. On 9 March Nick du Toit, a South African who helped with recruitment, weapons and logistics, and 14 others were arrested in Equatorial Guinea, and du Toit testified that Mann had recruited him to install Moto. The name comes from a letter Mann wrote from prison asking for "a large splodge of wonga", British slang for money.
On 13 January 2005 Mark Thatcher, son of the former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher, pleaded guilty in South Africa to attempting to breach its anti-mercenary law by agreeing to charter a helicopter he suspected might be used for mercenary activity. Al Jazeera reported he had paid $275,000 for the charter. He was fined 3 million rand, about $500,000, and given a four-year prison term suspended for five years.
Mann served three years in Zimbabwe and was then extradited to Equatorial Guinea, where he was sentenced in 2008 to more than 34 years. President Obiang pardoned him on 2 November 2009 and he returned to England, where he died in May 2025.

new-utopia.story:
New Utopia was a planned tax-free country on concrete platforms over the Misteriosa Bank, an underwater rise in the Caribbean about 115 miles west of the Cayman Islands. It was never built and existed only as an offer to investors. Howard Turney, who ran an anti-ageing clinic in Mexico, renamed himself Lazarus Long around 1995 after a character in Robert Heinlein's novels and promoted it. A website of more than 100 pages offered government bonds, meaning loans to the new country, at 9.5 percent interest, and promised currency returns as high as 200 percent.
Plans included 642 apartments and a casino. On 8 April 1999 the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which polices investment sales, filed suit. It alleged false statements about construction, the companies involved, the safety of the investment and the SEC's own inquiry. Judge Michael Burrage in Tulsa, Oklahoma, issued an emergency order freezing the money, which the Associated Press put near $100,000 at that stage.
On 20 January 2000 Long accepted a final judgment without contesting it and was barred from further violations. The SEC waived repayment of $24,000 plus interest because he swore he could not pay. The SEC says about $24,000 was raised, while encyclopedia entries claim $100 million. Long died in April 2012. His daughter announced a revival in 2017, and nothing is known to have come of it.

morac-songhrati-meads.story:
The Republic of Morac-Songhrati-Meads was a claim, made only in documents, to the Spratly Islands, a group of reefs and islets in the South China Sea that several countries dispute. Its supporters said a British sea captain, James George Meads, had claimed the islands in 1877 and called himself King James I, and that a rival branch of the family formed a Kingdom of Humanity in 1914. None of this has been shown to be true.
The first evidence that can be checked comes from 1946, when Morton F. Meads, the captain's supposed descendant and an American soldier, was discharged in Manila over illegal private business, mainly reselling army surplus. Philippine newspapers printed his stories about a family birthright. Those stories drew the attention of Filipino businessmen such as Tomás Cloma, who then raced to claim the islands for the Philippines.
The group never set up a settlement, and its activity was limited to items such as postage stamps. Meads asked the United Nations, the Republic of China and the Philippines for recognition in 1972 and got nowhere. By one account, the rest of its governing body drowned that year when Typhoon Ora sank their ship. In 1985 he sued the United States and others for $25 billion, and the case was never heard. His descendants were still making the claim in the 1990s.

freedomland-kalayaan.story:
Freedomland was a territory that a Filipino businessman claimed in the Spratly Islands in the South China Sea, which the Philippines later took over and now counts as its own. Tomás Cloma owned a fishing fleet and a maritime school. His brother Filemon reportedly found the area when a typhoon pushed his boats west of Palawan in 1947. On 11 May 1956 Filemon led 40 men in taking formal possession of 53 islands and islets some 380 miles west of Palawan, and they posted a Notice to the Whole World.
Tomás argued the area had no owner because Japan had given it up in the San Francisco peace treaty of 1951, and he declared the Free Territory of Freedomland on 21 May, with a capital on Flat Island from July. In October 1956 Taiwanese naval ships met Filemon's boat at North Danger Reef, and Taiwan later burned buildings and took property. The brothers then asked the Philippine government for support.
In 1972 President Ferdinand Marcos jailed Tomás for four months for impersonating an officer by using the title admiral. In August 1974 the group adopted a new constitution and renamed the territory Colonia. That December Tomás was arrested and made to sign over his rights to the Philippines for one peso. A 1978 decree made the area the Municipality of Kalayaan.

deepsea-ventures-claim.story:
In 1974 an American company, Deepsea Ventures Inc. of Gloucester Point, Virginia, claimed the sole right to mine a patch of the northeastern Pacific seabed that lay outside every country's control. The target was manganese nodules, potato-sized lumps of metal on the ocean floor, in a deposit covering 60,000 square kilometres. At the time no treaty said who could mine the deep seabed, because the Law of the Sea treaty, the main international agreement on use of the oceans, was still being negotiated.
On 15 November the company's president, John Flipse, sent a notice of discovery to Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, asking the American government for diplomatic protection, and recorded a copy at a local courthouse. Copies went to cabinet members, congressional committees, ambassadors of maritime countries, oceanographers and other companies. The magazine Reason called it the world's first ocean mining claim. The company promised commercial production within 15 years, running for 40 years.
It asserted exclusive rights to mine and sell the nodules, and said it was claiming no territory and was not asking the United States to do so. The 1982 treaty later put the area under an international authority. Mining is not known to have taken place under the claim, and no court is known to have ruled on it.

proteus-curacao.story:
Proteus is a planned undersea research station off the Caribbean island of Curaçao, proposed by Fabien Cousteau, grandson of the explorer Jacques Cousteau, through his company Proteus Ocean Group. He decided to build it after spending 31 days in the Aquarius undersea laboratory off Florida in 2014, and he describes it as a space station for the sea. It first reached the press in August 2020.
The main living spaces would be about 20 metres down, inside a marine park off the island's northeast coast, with a deeper satellite module at 70 metres. It is modular, meaning built from connected units, and could hold 12 people normally and up to 18 at a squeeze. Dive magazine reported that it needed US$60 million to build and US$75 million to run for its first three years, paid for by renting space to technology firms and research centres.
Curaçao's prime minister, Gilmar Pisas, announced that it was expected to be finished in 2026 near Fuik. A Boat International report in October 2024 said it was still in planning, with launch hoped for around 2027 and heavy funding still needed. An expert quoted there said going under water is very costly and has been harder to achieve than reaching the moon. It is not known to have been built.
It would sit in Curaçao's waters with the government's backing, and no one has claimed sovereignty over the seabed or the water above.

republic-of-kugelmugel.story:
The Republic of Kugelmugel is a spherical house eight metres across that its builder declared an independent country, now standing in the Prater park in Vienna, Austria. In 1971 the artist Edwin Lipburger and his son built it near Wiener Neustadt in Lower Austria without a building permit, which started a long dispute with the authorities. In August 1975 the township of Neudorfl offered it a home, and moving it by helicopter was discussed, but that did not happen.
Lipburger then declared the sphere an independent republic, with the date given as 19 December 1976, and issued passports. In 1979 he was sentenced to 10 weeks in prison for unlawful assumption of a public authority, the Austrian offence of acting as an official without the right to. In 1982 the building was dismantled and moved to the Prater, where it sits behind tall barbed-wire fences.
Helmut Zilk, who became mayor of Vienna in 1984, gave it what was called asylum. The city assumed the arrangement would be temporary, and the legal dispute continued. The republic claims 94 square metres and has a single address, 2 Antifaschismusplatz. Leadership of the republic passed to Nikolaus Lipburger in 2015 and to Linda Treiber, as president, in 2022, and the house remains in the Prater.
republic-of-kugelmugel.mechanism: Declaring a building a state does not remove the need for a building permit. When the founder acted as if he held public office, Austria used a criminal offence against false official acts.

rojava.story:
The Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria, also called Rojava, was a Kurdish-led self-governing region in north-eastern Syria that lasted from 2012 to 2026. It grew out of the Syrian civil war. In 2012 Kurdish-led forces took control of parts of the north-east in practice. In March 2016 Kurdish groups announced a federal system, and the region was later organised into sub-regions that at various times included Afrin, Jazira, Euphrates, Raqqa, Tabqa, Manbij and Deir ez-Zor.
Its armed force was the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). It ran some foreign relations but was not recognised as autonomous by Syria or by any other state, although the Parliament of Catalonia, a regional body in Spain, did recognise it. From 2016 Turkish forces and Turkish-backed Syrian rebels occupied parts of northern Syria in a series of operations. In January 2026 Syria's transitional government took back those areas and launched an offensive in the north-east, capturing up to 80 percent of the administration's land, and the rest was handed over under an agreement to merge it into the Syrian state.
On 20 August 2026 SDF commander Mazloum Abdi said the military, security and administrative bodies had been integrated. After an agreement with President Ahmed al-Sharaa, he announced the SDF's dissolution on 25 August, and Syrian state television said this also covered the autonomous administration.
rojava.mechanism: This self-rule, won during a civil war, lasted while the central government was weak and foreign backers stayed involved. It ended through a military offensive and a negotiated merger into the Syrian state.

iss-intergovernmental-agreement.story:
The International Space Station orbits Earth with people living on it and has no government of its own.
