A treaty signed on 29 January 1998 by the United States, Canada, Japan, Russia and the member countries of the European Space Agency divides legal authority among them. Under Article 5, each partner keeps legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens on board.
The European Space Agency describes this as treating those modules like part of the partners' territory, so European law applies inside Europe's Columbus laboratory, and national courts hear cases on liability and inventions. Article 22 covers crime. A Congressional Research Service paper explains that each country may prosecute its own citizens for what they do in any module. If misconduct endangers another country's citizen, or happens in or damages another partner's module, the suspect's country must consult the affected country.
The affected country may then prosecute if the suspect's country agrees or gives no assurance that it will prosecute. A Crew Code of Conduct agreed in September 2000 sets a chain of command. The station is still in orbit under these rules, with seven people on board in early November 2026. Each partner's law applies in its own modules, and no single legal authority covers the whole station.

planetary-resources-dsi.story:
Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries were two companies, announced in the early 2010s, that planned to mine asteroids. Their plans helped push governments to write laws on who owns what is mined in space. Planetary Resources announced itself in 2012 with prominent business backers, and nine months later Deep Space Industries, founded by entrepreneurs and space advocates, announced similar plans to find and extract materials such as water ice.
Both built small spacecraft, and both stood to gain when the United States in 2015 and Luxembourg in 2017 passed laws on who owns materials mined in space. Their money ran out before any mining began. In 2017 a funding round for Planetary Resources with a major mining company fell through, which led to large layoffs. In October 2018 the blockchain firm ConsenSys bought it on undisclosed terms and named only two of its people as staying.
On 1 January 2019 Bradford Space announced that it had bought Deep Space Industries, whose work by then was on small-satellite engines. Jeff Foust, writing in The Space Review, concluded that the asteroid mining boom had been a bubble. The laws they helped inspire remain in force after both firms were sold.
planetary-resources-dsi.mechanism: National laws on owning materials mined in space were written with these firms in mind, and those laws remain in force after the firms were sold. They came before any actual mining took place.

radio-veronica.story:
Radio Veronica was a Dutch pop radio station that broadcast from a ship off the coast of the Netherlands from 1960 to 1974. Dutch retailers of radios and appliances set it up to sell more receivers, by offering an alternative to the state-licensed stations in the town of Hilversum. Regular broadcasts began on 6 May 1960 from a former lightship, Borkum Riff, anchored off the coast, with programmes recorded in Hilversum and taken out to it.
It became the most popular station in the Netherlands. In 1964 the Dutch government passed a law against broadcasting from REM Island, an artificial structure at sea, and raided that island, but it left Veronica alone because of the station's popularity. A new ship, the trawler MV Norderney, took over that year. In May 1971 three men firebombed Mebo II, a rival broadcasting ship, and Veronica's directors were arrested over it.
Parliament then drew up a ban. On 2 April 1973 Norderney lost its anchor in a storm and ran aground at Scheveningen, two weeks before a planned rally, and a rival ship carried its programmes. The law passed anyway, and Veronica shut at 6 pm on 31 August 1974, hours before it took effect.

corpus-separatum-jerusalem.story:
Corpus separatum, Latin for 'separated body', was a United Nations plan to place Jerusalem and its surroundings under international government. It was part of the UN Partition Plan for Palestine, adopted by the General Assembly on 29 November 1947 as Resolution 181, which also proposed separate Arab and Jewish states. The city was to have special status because of its importance to Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and the idea drew on the Vatican's long concern for the Christian holy places.
The area ran from Abu Dis in the east to Bethlehem in the south, Ein Karim in the west and Shu'fat in the north. A governor appointed by the UN Trusteeship Council, the UN body overseeing territories not yet self-governing, would run it, and its founding law would be reviewed after ten years and put to a referendum. It was never carried out. Palestinian and other Arab leaders first rejected it, though Arab governments later supported it.
The British left on 14 May 1948 without setting up the regime, and the 1948 Arab-Israeli War left Israel holding the west of the city and Transjordan, now Jordan, the east. In December 1949 Israeli prime minister David Ben-Gurion declared the plan void, and the General Assembly reaffirmed it days later, but the statute approved in 1950 was never applied. In 2012 the European Parliament and the General Assembly expressed support for Jerusalem as a dual capital of Israel and a State of Palestine.

liftport.story:
LiftPort Group is a private company in Washington state, founded in April 2003 by Michael Laine, that set out to build a space elevator, a cable running from the ground into space with climbing machines carrying cargo along it. In 2005 it announced a plant in Millville, New Jersey, to make carbon nanotubes, a very strong material made of carbon atoms, and set a goal of launching an elevator in 2010.
The plant was never built. The company did run tests, including a 1,000-foot ribbon held up by a balloon in September 2005 with a machine climbing it, and in February 2006 it reported testing a mile of tether made of carbon fibre and fibreglass. In 2007 the company faced a penalty over an alleged illegal offering of its shares, and in February 2010 it settled with the State of Washington without a fine.
In 2011 Laine turned to an elevator on the Moon as a first step, and a 2012 Kickstarter campaign raised $110,353 from 3,468 backers. Many of them have reportedly asked what happened and received no reply. In April 2019 Laine admitted that little progress had been made despite more than $200,000 in seed funding. No elevator has been built.

stratobus.story:
Stratobus is a robotic airship designed to hover about 20 kilometres above the ground, higher than the jet stream and regular air traffic. It is being developed by the French space company Thales Alenia Space, and the French Ministry of Industry selected it for a national industrial programme. In 2015 Thales described a craft 100 metres long, weighing about 5 tons, able to carry up to 250 kilograms of equipment for five years with a couple of days a year on the ground for maintenance.
It planned a prototype in 2018 or 2019 and commercial sale around 2020, and it said flight tests had to come before certification and flight authorisation. Neither date was met. The defence publisher Janes later reported a French defence concept study for a larger design 115 metres long. In September 2025 Reuters quoted the head of Stratobus describing a balloon 142 metres long, and Aviation Week reported that the company had started building two reduced-scale test models. The aim is to be ready for use by 2031. No plans for people aboard have been reported.

nutopia.story:
Nutopia was a country with no land, announced by the musician John Lennon and the artist Yoko Ono at a press conference in New York City on 2 April 1973, the day after they signed its declaration. The text says Nutopia has no land, no boundaries, no passports, only people, and no laws other than cosmic ones. Anyone could become a citizen by declaring awareness of it.
All citizens were to be ambassadors, and the founders asked for diplomatic immunity, the legal protection foreign diplomats have from a host country's courts, along with recognition from the United Nations. Lennon had just received an order to leave the United States, and the new country was partly a way to answer it. Nutopia's flag was a white handkerchief, and its anthem, on Lennon's 1973 album Mind Games, is four seconds of silence.
Its embassy was an apartment at 1 White Street in Manhattan and later a plaque on a kitchen door at the Dakota building. No government is known to have granted the immunity. The deportation order was overturned in 1975 and Lennon received a green card, the US permit for permanent residence, in 1976. Since April 2024 people have been able to declare citizenship through a website.

uae-japan-space-resources.story:
These are laws from the United Arab Emirates and Japan that allow companies to use materials mined in space, following the United States and Luxembourg. The Emirates' Federal Law No. 12 of 2019 covers licensing, registering spacecraft, liability and insurance, along with rules on building facilities on other planets and on using space resources. It had come into force by early 2020. Japan's parliament then passed Act No. 83 of 2021, on business activities in exploring and developing space resources, which made Japan the fourth country to pass such a law. Article 5 is headed Acquisition of Ownership of Space Resources, and according to the news site Atalayar the law lets Japanese companies find, extract and own minerals from the surface and subsurface of the Moon, Mars or other bodies. Japan's Hayabusa 2 mission had returned a few grams of dust from the asteroid Ryugu in December 2020, which showed that extraction is possible on a small scale.
Together with the American and Luxembourg laws, these acts form a growing group of countries treating mining as a lawful use of space. No international treaty authorises this, and no court has tested the laws.

havenco.story:
HavenCo was an internet hosting company based on Sealand, a former wartime sea fort off the English coast whose occupants call it an independent country. Its American founders opposed government censorship of the internet and wanted to keep customers' data on servers beyond the reach of other countries' courts, an arrangement known as a data haven. Michael Bates, son of Sealand's self-styled ruler, set the business up in August 2000 by buying a dormant British company and renaming it HavenCo Limited, so it was registered in the country it hoped to escape.
It later moved its registration to Cyprus. Investors included Avi Freedman and Joichi Ito. The company hoped to serve online casinos, pornography distributors and firms wanting records that no court order could reach, and it advertised first-world infrastructure with third-world regulation. Law professor James Grimmelmann, who wrote its history, found that the dot-com crash cut Sealand's internet links more than any government did. Co-founder Ryan Lackey left in 2002 after disputes with the Bates family over management, and he said Sealand had probably nationalized the company, meaning taken it over.
He could not sue, because Sealand's monarch headed its courts and going to a foreign court would have undercut the claim that Sealand was independent. The new management banned activities against international law. Operations stopped and the website went offline in November 2008. In 2013 Freedman announced a revival with servers in the European Union and the United States and some stored data on Sealand. The revival is not known to have succeeded, and the company is listed as defunct.

minerva-1982-and-fiji-tonga.story:
The Minerva Reefs are two submerged atolls, or ring-shaped coral reefs, between Fiji and Tonga, which Tonga annexed in 1972 to stop a private group founding a country there. In 1982 a group of Americans led by Morris 'Bud' Davis, the former provisional president of that Republic of Minerva, tried to occupy them again. Tongan troops forced them off after three weeks. No later group is reported to have taken possession, and Reason magazine later described the structure as more or less reclaimed by the sea.
The argument then passed to the two states, because a recognised reef can give its owner rights over the surrounding waters. In 2005 Fiji declared that it did not recognise any maritime claims by Tonga based on the reefs under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the 1982 treaty on states' rights at sea. That November Fiji complained to the International Seabed Authority, the body that oversees the deep ocean floor, and Tonga lodged a counter-claim.
In 2010 and again in May 2011 Fiji's navy destroyed navigation equipment on the reefs, and in June 2011 Tongan navy ships went to replace it. In July 2014 Tonga's lands minister proposed giving the reefs to Fiji in exchange for the Lau Islands. The dispute is not known to have been settled.

mcclean-rockall.story:
Rockall is a tiny bare rock in the North Atlantic, west of Scotland. Britain claimed it in 1955 and made it part of Scotland in 1972. Ireland has never claimed the rock itself but disputes Britain's position. Tom McClean, a Dublin-born adventurer who had served in Britain's Parachute Regiment and Special Air Service, went to live on it to strengthen Britain's claim, so his aim was the opposite of founding a breakaway state.
He stayed from 26 May to 4 July 1985 in what one account calls a wooden box, a record 40 days alone. Whether people can live on Rockall matters because of the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the main treaty on ocean rights. Under it, a rock that cannot support human life or economic activity gets no exclusive economic zone (a belt of sea up to 200 nautical miles wide where a country controls fish and minerals) and no continental shelf (rights over the nearby seabed).
The statement that his stay reaffirmed Britain's claim has been questioned. Greenpeace activists passed his total in 1997 with 42 days, and Nick Hancock reached 45 days alone in 2014. Britain still claims the rock and 12 nautical miles of sea around it, and Ireland still disputes this.

coral-sea-kingdom.story:
The Gay and Lesbian Kingdom of the Coral Sea Islands was a protest state on the Coral Sea Islands, small uninhabited islands and reefs east of the Great Barrier Reef that belong to Australia. In May 2004 the Australian government brought a bill to Parliament defining marriage as between a man and a woman. In response, on 14 June 2004 activists led by Dale Parker Anderson raised the rainbow flag on Cato Island, the territory's highest point, and claimed the islands as a homeland for gay and lesbian people.
A plaque there records the date, and a campsite called Heaven was named the capital. In a scheme modelled on Israel's Law of Return, which lets Jews settle in Israel, any gay or lesbian person could gain residence and citizenship. Anderson was elected administrator and then declared emperor. The scholar Judy Lattas of Macquarie University, who interviewed him in 2007, treats it as a real secession and argues that gay nationalism may need territorial claims to secure rights.
Others describe it as a symbolic protest. Its leaders dissolved the kingdom on 17 November 2017, after the Yes result in Australia's postal survey on same-sex marriage.

seapods-panama.story:
SeaPods are small floating homes built by the company Ocean Builders at a marina on the Caribbean coast of Panama. Ocean Builders had first tried to live beyond national law. Its 2019 seastead off Phuket was raided by the Thai navy, and its 2020 plan to turn a cruise ship into a floating community, the MS Satoshi, collapsed because no insurer would cover it. It then turned to homes inside a state's waters.
In September 2022 the Panamanian newspaper Panamá América reported houses being built at Linton Bay Marina in the province of Colón, designed with the Dutch architect Koen Olthuis and his firm Waterstudio. The company took reservations for a $100 deposit, with prices from about $295,000 to $1.5 million. A SeaPod stands above the water on a float tethered to the seabed by anchors, runs mainly on solar power, collects rain water and carries Starlink satellite internet and more than 100 sensors.
At the unveiling on 22 September 2022, in front of an audience that included Panama's president, Laurentino Cortizo, the prototype tipped over with people inside. The company blamed a failed bilge pump, a pump that clears water from the hull, and denied that the home sank, and AP reported no injuries. By June 2023 a Condé Nast Traveler writer stayed in one off Panama's Caribbean coast as among the first guests, and a Smithsonian researcher told the writer that floating pods touch the seabed less than bungalows on pillars. The company does not claim independence from Panama. The number of permanent residents is not known.

blueseed.story:
Blueseed was a company in Palo Alto, California, founded on 31 July 2011 by Max Marty, Dario Mutabdzija and Dan Dascalescu, that planned to house startup founders on a ship anchored 12 nautical miles off the California coast near Silicon Valley. That spot lies just outside the US territorial sea, the belt of water a state fully controls, in the contiguous zone, where a coastal state has only limited powers.
The point was to get around US immigration law. Foreign entrepreneurs could work on the ship without an H-1B work visa and travel to the mainland on easier business or tourist visas. The project received wide press coverage and a promise of investment from Peter Thiel, the technology investor, who did not invest in the seed round, the first stage of funding. It reported US$300,000 in seed funding, some Bitcoin investments and $9 million from an undisclosed investor, and said it would lease a ship.
Its launch date moved from the third quarter of 2013 to late 2014, on the assumption that $18 million more would come in. The money did not arrive, and the project went on hold in 2013. The company reportedly resumed in 2020 as a business accelerator, a programme that helps new firms, and dropped the ship.

life-at-sea.story:
Life at Sea Cruises was a company, with Miray Cruises as its parent, that sold a three-year round-the-world voyage in which passengers would live aboard at prices it said rivalled ordinary living costs. It made no claim of sovereignty, but it shows what buyers risked when they paid a private company for a home at sea before any ship existed. The voyage was due to leave Istanbul, Turkey, on 1 November 2023.
Shortly before that, the date moved to 11 November and the port to Amsterdam, and then to 30 November. On 17 November passengers were told the cruise was off, and the company admitted it had no ship. Some of the buyers of the 111 cabins sold were already in Istanbul, and others said they had sold or let their homes and given away their possessions.
Most had spent tens of thousands of dollars. The company promised repayment in monthly instalments from mid-December to late February, and offered to pay for flights home and hotels until 1 December. By January 2024 only four passengers had received refunds, and 78 customers asked the US attorney in southern Florida, the federal prosecutor there, to open a criminal investigation over about $16 million in deposits. How that request ended is not known.

oceanix-busan.story:
Oceanix Busan is a proposed floating neighbourhood off Busan, a port city in South Korea, backed by the city government and UN-Habitat, the United Nations agency for cities. Its stated aim is to give coastal cities new land as seas rise and housing costs grow. UN-Habitat said two of every five people live within 100 kilometres of a coast and that 90 percent of mega cities are vulnerable to rising seas.
On 18 November 2021 Busan, UN-Habitat and the company OCEANIX signed an agreement to build a prototype, with about $200 million anticipated as the cost. On 26 April 2022, at UN Headquarters in New York, the three partners unveiled the design for what they called the world's first prototype sustainable floating city, and said they were on track to deliver it. Unlike earlier projects to settle the sea, it would stand in South Korean waters under a city government, with no attempt to leave any state's law.
In October 2023 the Busan broadcaster KNN reported that a conference on the project gave no concrete financing or construction plans. Construction is not known to have started, no one is known to live there, and it is listed as not yet built.

dominion-of-melchizedek.story:
The Dominion of Melchizedek is a self-declared country, regarded by American regulators as non-existent, that has been used to sell passports, bank licences and financial paper. The American Mark Pedley declared it in 1990, possibly with his father David, who had been convicted of financial crimes in the 1970s. Mark had his own convictions, including a $6 million currency fraud in 1986, and his parole was revoked in 1991 for promoting a fictitious country.
Melchizedek had no fixed home. It claimed Malpelo, a Colombian island, then Karitane Shoal in the South Pacific, a place that appears to have been invented and that its spokesman described as 14 square miles of sandy beaches. It also claimed French-owned Clipperton Island, Bokak Atoll in the Marshall Islands and part of Antarctica. About 300 bank licences were claimed to have been sold by the end of the 1990s, and in 1991 shell banks in Washington, D.C., tried to get loans with fake Melchizedek securities and were shut down.
One investment scheme took over $4 million from at least 1,400 people. Passports sold for up to $3,500, and three people posing as officials were arrested in the Philippines in 1998. That April the Marshall Islands government condemned its claims as fraudulent. One source puts the total raised above $500 million. Pedley pleaded guilty to share manipulation in 2010, and his wife Pearlasia Gamboa, Melchizedek's president, lost a $1.8 million civil judgment that year. It is not known to have been formally dissolved.
dominion-of-melchizedek.mechanism: A claim to be a sovereign state, one answerable to no other, can be used to sell passports and financial paper, with claims to reefs and shoals and no one living there. Ordinary fraud law applies to the people selling them.

kingdom-of-enenkio.story:
The Kingdom of EnenKio is a self-declared country claiming Wake Island, a remote Pacific atoll controlled by the United States since 1899. The Marshall Islands also claims the atoll, which it calls Ānen Kio, on the basis of oral legends and songs. In 1994 Robert F. Moore, a Honolulu resident who said he acted for a Marshallese chief, Murjel Hermios, announced that an independent kingdom existed there.
It issued passports, and in 1997 the Marshall Islands Journal reported that it had declared war on the United States and was asking for Marshallese support. On 23 April 1998 the Marshall Islands government issued a formal note condemning its claims, saying its representatives were not citizens and had no right to speak for Marshallese landowners. Moore then turned to investors. He marketed $1 billion in Enenkio Gold War Bonds online, saying they were backed by gold and promising 10 percent compound interest after five years.
The Securities and Exchange Commission, the American regulator of investments, said no gold or other backing existed and the bonds had not been registered as the law required. In October 2000 it won a court order from Judge Susan Mollway in Honolulu that froze his assets and required him to account for the money. How the case ended is not known, and no state recognises the kingdom.

liberstad.story:
Liberstad is a planned private city on three parcels of land totalling about 150 hectares in rural southern Norway, near the village of Bjelland and a few hours from Kristiansand. Its backers wanted to provide public services without a government, with minimal rules and no taxes, following the ideas of the free-market writers Mises, Hayek and Rothbard. They sold land from 2015, in bitcoin or Norwegian krone, at between about $9,400 for 1,000 square metres and $47,100 for 5,000 square metres.
A company called Liberstad Drift AS was to keep the land records and act as custodian. A 2017 Cointelegraph report said development would begin on 1 June if enough plots sold. The Startup Societies Foundation, a group that promotes such projects, reported that 120 people had bought land. It said the project does not demand sovereignty of any type and described it as an experiment in how society could work. It is not known to have a finished settlement or a permanent population.

bitcoin-city.story:
Bitcoin City is a planned city in La Unión, El Salvador, at the foot of the Conchagua volcano. President Nayib Bukele announced it in November 2021, after his country had adopted the digital currency bitcoin. Geothermal power from the volcano was to be used to mine bitcoin, the computer process that creates new coins. The city was to be circular, like a coin, and almost free of taxes apart from a 13 percent value-added tax, a sales tax, half of which would pay off bonds.
Money was to come from a $1 billion "volcano bond" involving the state power company LaGeo, with half for the city and half for buying bitcoin. Some bond buyers might receive Salvadoran citizenship. NBC reported that analysts paid more attention to the bonds than to the city. Delays in financing and construction followed. Under a later deal with the International Monetary Fund, a global lender to governments in financial trouble, businesses no longer had to accept bitcoin and taxes could no longer be paid in it.
The Week described this as ending bitcoin's run as effective legal tender, meaning money everyone must accept. An airport in the plan was expected to start operating in 2027, according to a 2025 source. The city itself is not known to have been built.

tongasat.story:
Tongasat is a company that files for and rents out satellite positions on behalf of Tonga, a small kingdom in the South Pacific. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a United Nations agency, assigns places in geostationary orbit, the ring above the equator where a satellite stays over one spot, to countries that apply. In 1987 Matt Nilson, a businessman who had moved to Tonga from San Diego, persuaded the king, through Princess Pilolevu, that even a tiny country could apply.
The government authorised the venture in April 1988, and in March 1990 Nilson applied for 16 of the 180 slots then available. Intelsat, a satellite operator, and the United States objected. The ITU agreed in March 1991 after he cut the request to six, and Tonga eventually held nine. The plan was to rent each slot for $2 million a year, with half the profit going to the government.
A company called Rimsat rented slots in 1992, and Nilson was fired in February 1994 after an audit found he owned Rimsat shares. China later wanted the slot at 130 degrees East, and Tonga gave way in exchange for grant aid, part of which went to Tongasat. On 17 August 2018 Lord Chief Justice Paulsen ruled that the company had unlawfully received over $46 million in public money.
In 2019 the court refused Tongasat's request to bring new evidence to its appeal and ordered it to pay about $15,000 as security for costs by 1 November, or the appeal would be put on hold. How the appeal finally ended is not known.

flags-of-convenience-space.story:
A flag of convenience is a practice from shipping, where an owner registers a merchant ship in a country with light rules and flies that country's flag. Lawyers have asked whether spacecraft can do the same. Adrian Taghdiri wrote a 2013 note in the Boston University Journal of Science and Technology Law, as space tourism was starting, predicting that some countries would set loose rules to attract private space companies.
He warned of environmental harm, more debris and danger to passengers. Space law limits the effect without removing it. Under the Outer Space Treaty, the country that registers a spacecraft keeps legal authority over it and its crew. Any launching state, meaning a country that launches a craft or pays for its launch, stays liable for damage. So a cheap registry cannot remove the liability of the country whose soil was used.
A presentation at a symposium of the UN's space law subcommittee in Vienna in 2016 set out the shipping idea and asked how it fits space objects. The closest working example involves orbital slots, the positions assigned to satellites. The business of Tonga's company Tongasat has been described as in effect a flag of convenience for space, and later filings came from Gibraltar, Papua New Guinea and Bermuda. The practice has not been tested in any court.

moon-express-faa.story:
Moon Express is a private American company, formed in 2010 by Robert Richards, Naveen Jain and Barney Pell, that aimed to win the Google Lunar XPRIZE contest and eventually mine the Moon. In 2016 it wanted to land its MX-1E craft, about the size of a coffee table, on the Moon. No US agency was clearly in charge of private missions beyond Earth orbit, though Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty requires a country to authorise and continually supervise its companies in space.
So the company asked the Federal Aviation Administration to review the payload. On 20 July 2016 the agency gave a favorable payload determination, the first for a commercial payload meant to land on the Moon. It did so after consulting the State Department and NASA, and found no threat to safety, national security, foreign policy or treaty obligations. Lawyers at the group TechFreedom questioned whether one review letter met Article VI, and they urged Congress to pass a clear law.
The mission never flew. No team in the contest was able to launch by the deadline of 31 March 2018, and the company shelved its lander plans and turned to competing for NASA delivery contracts. Its activity after 2020 is not known.

wirtland.story:
Wirtland was a self-declared country that existed only on the internet, founded on 14 August 2008. It called itself the first internet-based sovereign state and an experiment on whether a country can be legitimate without land. Its own announcement in 2009 claimed about 700 citizens from all five continents. It sold real objects to give itself a physical presence, including silver coins struck with its web address, stamps and a national identity card open to anyone over 18.
In January 2010 a post on the international law blog The View From LL2 described a Wirtland press release proposing to ask Nauru, a small Pacific island country, to transfer a piece of its territory. The blogger noted that Nauru's recognition had gone to the highest bidder before, but said the scheme could never work and that Wirtland was no sovereign, with few citizens and no power to tax. No land is known to have changed hands, and no activity is known in 2026.

citydao.story:
CityDAO is an online group that bought 40 acres of rural Wyoming, in the United States, with the stated aim of building a city of the future with all its records on a blockchain, a shared public ledger. A DAO, or decentralised autonomous organisation, is a group that makes decisions and holds money through software on a blockchain. Scott Fitsimones started the idea with a tweet in July 2021, just after Wyoming's new DAO law took effect, because Wyoming was then the only state letting such a group hold property as a company.
In October 2021 the group bought the land, called Parcel 0, west of Clark and about 30 minutes from Cody, for around $100,000. Members hold a digital token called a Citizenship NFT and vote on proposals. In June 2022 CityDAO told a Wyoming legislative committee it had about 6,500 citizens and floated the idea of incorporating an actual city, if counties agreed, with deeds, titles and tax records on the blockchain.
It has never claimed independence, and citizen here only means someone who holds the token. In May 2023 the local press reported that the land was undeveloped, with a well and a flat building area, and that zoning rules may allow only one house on each 40-acre lot. What has since become of the project is not known.

afropolitan.story:
Afropolitan is a company in the San Francisco Bay Area that has marketed itself as a digital nation for the African diaspora. It began in 2016 as a networking and events business for wealthy members of the diaspora. In May 2022, its founders Eche Emole and Chika Uwazie announced a four-part plan for what the tech news site Built In reported as the world's first digital nation, aimed at fostering the Black community.
They drew on the network-state idea of the entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan, who argues that online communities can grow into countries. They compared it to Facebook as a country, with its own laws, currency and culture. The company raised $2.1 million in seed funding, money from early investors, and in September 2022 Uwazie rang the closing bell at the New York Stock Exchange. A critical 2025 article on the website Africa Is a Country found that three years on, the founders ran a podcast and three services launched in late 2024, namely a dating service, paid mentoring and an event-booking app.
The writer said the digital nation idea served as a hook for investors. It is not known to have any territory, passport or legal status, and Afropolitan continues as a company.

second-life-embassies.story:
In 2007 a few real countries opened embassies in Second Life, an online 3D world where people move around as animated figures. Sweden announced its plan in January and was to open on 30 May with a copy of the House of Sweden in Washington, built through the Swedish Institute, a government body that promotes the country abroad, for 400,000 kronor, about $57,000. The Maldives got there a few days earlier and put its own embassy on Diplomacy Island, a virtual diplomatic quarter.
Foreign Minister Carl Bildt then opened Sweden's in a ceremony held both online and in person. Estonia joined later that year, with Foreign Minister Urmas Paet citing the importance of the internet for communication and planning lectures and art shows. These countries used the embassies for publicity and cultural outreach, and the embassies added nothing to their legal status and created no territory. Whether any still operates is not known.

uae-iceberg-project.story:
This was a plan to tow a large iceberg from the Southern Ocean to the United Arab Emirates, a desert country on the Persian Gulf, for its fresh water. Abdulla Alsheni, an Emirati businessman who owned National Adviser Bureau Limited, announced it in 2017. The iceberg would come from the area of Heard Island to the coast of Fujairah and might yield 20 billion gallons of water.
The idea was older. In 1977 Saudi Arabia's Prince Mohammad al Faisal set up a company, Iceberg Transport International, for the same purpose, and that plan was never carried out. Alsheni presented his project to two UAE ministries, with a trial planned for early 2022 and a final tow in late 2023, at a cost of $100 to 150 million. The project's website claimed that under the freedom of the high seas, the rule that open ocean belongs to no country, anyone may take icebergs for private use.
In a 2022 article in the journal Ius Novum, the legal writer Mateusz Osiecki tested that claim. He concluded that a free-floating iceberg is probably no state's property, noted that writers hold three different views, and set out the duties under the 1991 Environmental Protocol to the Antarctic Treaty. He also noted that the UAE belongs to neither the Antarctic Treaty system nor the Law of the Sea treaty. No tow is known to have taken place.

aquatica-chamberland.story:
Aquatica was a proposal for a permanent human settlement on the sea floor, put forward by Dennis Chamberland, an aquanaut (a person who lives under water for long stretches) and bioengineer with thirty years at NASA. He described it as the first underwater settlement meant for permanent colonization, and spoke of children born under water, with schools and hospitals. He had commanded seven NASA underwater missions, grown crops in controlled settings on the ocean floor, and built a two-person habitat off Key Largo, Florida, that the film director James Cameron visited.
The first step, reported in February 2011, was to be a four-person underwater house called Leviathan, expected to be lowered to the seabed the following year. Its stated purpose was for residents to monitor and protect the ocean. The report gave no site, budget or legal basis, and Leviathan is not known to have been placed. Any seabed divers can reach from a shore base would most likely be on some country's continental shelf, the shallow sea floor off its coast, where that country keeps its rights over the bottom.

maldives-floating-city.story:
Maldives Floating City is a planned housing project on a 200-hectare lagoon about 10 minutes by boat from Malé, the capital of the Maldives, a low-lying island nation in the Indian Ocean. It is promoted as an answer to rising seas, since homes that float would rise with the water. The government signed it with the Dutch developer Dutch Docklands in 2010. It stalled after a change of government in February 2012 and was signed again on 8 May 2019, when five lagoons were allotted to the company.
The deal was revised on 23 June 2022. A ministry reply reported by Atoll Times said no work had begun on the lagoons, none had been reclaimed and two had been sold, and Economy Minister Fayyaz Ismail called the project a scam. In June 2023 the company said the plan had changed at the government's request, with first prices lowered to about $100,000, work starting that August and completion in early 2028.
Reports differ on progress. One said no mockup had been shown despite three announced dates, and a February 2023 report said a mockup could be seen in the Hulhumalé lagoon. In May 2024 Newsweek published satellite images it described as showing construction, and lead architect Koen Olthuis expected first residents within 14 months. Other accounts give about 5,000 units for 20,000 residents, opening in 2027. Finished homes or residents have not been confirmed.

independence-referendum-record.story:
An independence referendum is a public vote in which residents decide whether their territory should become a separate country. A Yes vote does not always bring independence. Wikipedia's table lists about 123 such votes up to November 2026, starting with Chile in 1817. Counting its outcomes gives 59 votes ending in a No, 31 in a Yes followed by independence and recognition from other states, 16 in a Yes with no independence, and 12 in a Yes where the territory took control on the ground without general recognition.
The rest ended in a status linked to another state, a disputed independence or continuing negotiation. Western Australia voted Yes in 1933 and stayed in Australia. Nevis, in the Caribbean, voted Yes in 1998 and fell short of the two-thirds majority required. Quebec voted No in 1980 and 1995. Iraqi Kurdistan voted Yes in 2005 and 2017 without result. Votes held on terms agreed with the state being left can be binding and accepted abroad. Votes held without its consent can lead to one-sided declarations of independence and states that only some countries recognise.

bougainville-2019.story:
Bougainville is an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea in the South Pacific that voted for independence in 2019 and is still waiting for it. It was made a province in 1976 after Papua New Guinea became independent. A civil war from 1988 to 1998 ended with a 2001 peace agreement that promised a referendum. The vote ran from 23 November to 7 December 2019 and offered a choice of greater autonomy or independence.
Independence won 176,928 votes to 3,043, or 98.31%, with turnout of 87.38%, though press and parliamentary reports in 2026 give the share as 97.7%. The vote was not binding, and Papua New Guinea's national parliament has the final decision. In July 2021 the two governments agreed that Bougainville would become independent by 2027, subject to that parliament's approval. In July 2026 a forum of Bougainville leaders recommended 1 September 2030 as the target date.
The result was tabled in parliament on 27 August 2026, and Prime Minister James Marape said the two governments would consult in October to set a date for the vote. Minister Manasseh Makiba said a yes vote would start a transitional phase of self-government and would not bring immediate independence. The majority required is disputed. The national government says two-thirds or three-quarters of an absolute majority, the governing coalition has asked for 89 MPs, and the Bougainville government argues for 60 seats.
AAP, an Australian news agency, reports that Bougainville's government plans to declare sovereignty by 2030 if parliament delays further. By November 2026 no date for the vote had been reported.

biafra-1967.story:
Biafra was a breakaway republic in south-eastern Nigeria that existed from 1967 to 1970. It covered Nigeria's former Eastern Region and had about 13.5 million people, mainly Igbo with sizeable Ijaw, Efik, Ibibio and other populations. After ethnic tension, military coups and a 1966 pogrom against Igbo people, the region's governor, Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu, declared independence on 30 May 1967. Nigeria's military moved to retake the territory, which started the Nigerian Civil War.
Five states recognised Biafra officially, Gabon, Haiti, Côte d'Ivoire, Tanzania and Zambia. France, Portugal, Israel, South Africa and Rhodesia treated it as a state in practice and gave covert military support. Biafra also issued its own pound. Around two million Biafran civilians are estimated to have died in nearly three years of war. Ojukwu fled to Côte d'Ivoire, Philip Effiong oversaw the surrender, and the territory rejoined Nigeria on 15 January 1970. It remains part of Nigeria, and Igbo nationalism has grown more militant since the 1990s.

republic-of-new-afrika.story:
The Republic of New Afrika is a Black nationalist organisation in the United States that seeks an independent country in the Black Belt of the American South. It also demands reparations from the US government for slavery and the Jim Crow segregation laws, and a vote of African Americans on their citizenship. The Malcolm X Society, a Detroit group, called a Black Government Conference in Detroit on 31 March 1968, attended by about 500 people.
It adopted a declaration of independence, a constitution and a provisional government. Robert F. Williams, then in exile in Cuba, was chosen as first president, with Gaidi Obadele (Milton Henry) and Betty Shabazz, the widow of Malcolm X, as vice presidents. The group claimed Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina as 'subjugated national territory' and announced a capital on a member's farm in Hinds County, Mississippi.
Shootouts followed at New Bethel Baptist Church in Detroit in 1969 and in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1971, in which law-enforcement officers were killed and injured. Members were prosecuted and said they acted in self-defence. The organisation declined in the early 1970s, mainly because of government raids and mass arrests that jailed its leaders. Chokwe Lumumba, elected a vice president in 1971, became a lawyer and was mayor of Jackson from 2013 until his death in 2014. The group still lists officers, though its current activity is not known.

zhitomirsky-floating-islands.story:
The Floating Islands of Venus was a 1971 proposal by the Soviet engineer and science fiction writer Sergei Zhitomirsky for cities floating in the atmosphere of Venus, high above its hostile surface. He thought the technology used in zeppelins and hot air balloons could keep stations afloat some 50 or 60 kilometres above the surface, where temperature and other conditions were thought to be comfortable for people.
It is an early version of the idea, and Soviet scientists were suggesting settlement of the Venusian atmosphere at least as early as 1971. In 1991 Paul Birch suggested a related design, two-part domes filled with hydrogen or helium, in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society. None of these was built, and Zhitomirsky is not known to have claimed ownership of any part of Venus.

icarus-interstellar.story:
Icarus Interstellar is a volunteer nonprofit, registered in Alaska in February 2011, that studies how to send craft to other stars. It grew from Project Icarus, a five-year study of a fusion-powered starship started in September 2009 by Kelvin Long and Richard Obousy. That study built on Project Daedalus, a design from the 1970s by the British Interplanetary Society, a space advocacy group. The nonprofit's stated mission is to achieve interstellar flight before the year 2100, aiming at stars within 15 light-years or habitable planets within 22.
Its projects included Hyperion, on ships for many generations, and Persephone, which studied ecosystems for a ship 20 kilometres long and 5 kilometres across, housing 50 to 500 people. A Starship Congress in Dallas in August 2013 drew nearly 200 people, and another was scheduled for September 2015 at Drexel University. Its activity after 2015 is not known, and it has built no ship.

barbados-metaverse-embassy.story:
This is a plan by the Caribbean country of Barbados to open an embassy in the metaverse, meaning online 3D worlds where people move around as animated figures. On 14 November 2021 its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade signed an agreement with Decentraland, a virtual world with over 90,000 plots of land bought with cryptocurrency. Talks with two other platforms, Somnium Space and SuperWorld, were being finalised.
Gabriel Abed, a crypto entrepreneur and Barbados's ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, brokered the deal. The embassy would offer services such as electronic visas, and the country planned to declare its virtual land sovereign, meaning under its own authority. Avinash Persaud, special envoy to Prime Minister Mia Mottley, called it the first official embassy or lookout post in the metaverse and promised a report in twelve months.
A CoinDesk opinion piece called the idea a gimmick and asked why a website would not do. An opening was first expected around January 2022, and in February a newsletter still described it as coming soon. An article from June 2022 said it was tentatively scheduled for later that month. It has not been confirmed that the embassy opened or that the promised report appeared.

liberland-metaverse.story:
The Liberland Metaverse is a planned online 3D city for Liberland, a self-declared country on land between Serbia and Croatia. The Czech activist Vít Jedlička declared Liberland in 2015, and no state recognises it. Serbia's foreign ministry has called it a frivolous act needing no further comment. Croatia controls access to the land. In early 2022 the architecture firm Zaha Hadid Architects, under its principal Patrik Schumacher, released designs for the virtual city, with curving buildings, a City Hall, a plaza and an exhibition centre, hosted on a platform called Mytaverse.
Buyers could purchase virtual land and set up businesses there, and they would also get a stake in the physical Liberland. Schumacher said the aim was to support Liberland's development as a libertarian micronation and to make a meeting place for cryptocurrency and online developers. He also argued that open virtual worlds run by their communities will beat those run by corporations. In November 2022 press reports still described Liberland as about to become a country in the metaverse. How many plots were sold, and whether the city is in use, is not known.

vitalia.story: Vitalia was a temporary village focused on longevity, the science of living longer, held in February 2024 in Próspera, a zone in Honduras with its own legal rules. It had a laboratory for biohacking, meaning self-experiment to improve the body, along with workout groups and a biomedical hackathon, a contest to build projects quickly. Its organisers hoped it would lead to a permanent home base, and it is listed as a spin-off of Zuzalu, an earlier pop-up village. It ended after its 2024 session, and it is not known to have a permanent base.

zuitzerland.story:
Zuitzerland is a temporary village for technologists and researchers, held at Laax, a mountain resort in Switzerland. It grew out of Zuzalu, a two-month gathering in Montenegro in 2023, and out of defensive accelerationism, a movement that wants to speed up technology that protects people from harm. Its organisers call it a testing ground for a network state, meaning an online community that hopes to gain its own land and rules, and they say Switzerland's decentralised system suits the experiment.
A residency ran from 1 to 26 May 2025, with a summit on 17 to 19 May whose announced speakers included Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin. The Network State Atlas, a directory of such projects, lists it as active since 2024 and gives about 150 people per event. The organisers say they are building a permanent hub in Switzerland. Whether that hub exists is not known, and the group is not known to have claimed legal independence.

shanhaiwoo.story: ShanhaiWoo is a pop-up city, a temporary community that gathers in one place for a limited period and calls itself a city. A list of such gatherings by the newsletter Agartha places it in China and Thailand, and a report by IOSG counts it among the communities that met in Chiang Mai, Thailand, in October 2024. Neither names its founders or says how many people attended, and what it has done since is not known.

nova-roma.story:
Nova Roma is an international non-profit organisation that aims to restore the religion, culture and values of ancient Rome. It was formed in 1998 and later incorporated in the US state of Maine, and it offers a community for re-enactors, scholars and fans of ancient Rome. It calls itself a sovereign nation and is organised like the Roman Republic, with a senate, elected officials and laws passed by members' votes.
Latin is its official language, ancient Roman religion is its state religion alongside a guarantee of freedom of religion, and groups in different countries can form local branches called provinces. It minted coins in 2000 and 2005. Some outside observers class it as a micronation, a small self-declared state that other states do not recognise. It claims no territory, and its members go on living under the laws of their own countries.
Its most recent dated activity is a twentieth-anniversary celebration in Rome, and what it does now has not been confirmed.

obsidia.story:
The Ambulatory Free States of Obsidia is a feminist micronation, a small self-declared state that no government recognises, founded in 2015 by Karo Yagjian, who holds the title Grand Marshal. Yagjian was inspired partly by a summit of micronations called MicroCon and took a piece of obsidian, a black volcanic rock, and declared it independent. The nation's whole territory is two slabs of obsidian about the size of a book, carried in a blue and pink briefcase usually based in Oakland, California.
It is described as a mobile nation and art project that promotes gender equality and LGBTQ rights and opposes capitalism and borders. Anyone can become a citizen by reciting an oath and performing a salute, though cisgender men cannot serve in its government. In November 2021 Huck magazine estimated about 250 citizens, roughly 50 with passports, and reported satellite embassies in Hong Kong and Germany. Its present activity has not been confirmed.

austenasia.story:
The Empire of Austenasia is a micronation, a tiny self-declared country, based in a house in the London Borough of Sutton in England. Jonathan Austen, a teenage student, and his father Terry founded it on 20 September 2008 by sending a declaration of independence for their house in Carshalton to their local Member of Parliament, Tom Brake. Terry became Emperor and Jonathan Prime Minister. It claims to succeed the Roman Empire and has adopted Roman touches such as consuls and a senate.
It has grown as new citizens declared their own properties part of it, including houses in Britain, a holiday home in the Hebrides, part of a university campus in Australia, and places in the United States, Turkey and India. In May 2011 Jonathan met Brake, who asked Foreign Secretary William Hague what criteria Britain uses to recognise new states. After several other emperors, Jonathan took the throne in 2013.
Jonathan stepped back in April 2024 and handed the running of it to a Prince Regent, Aggelos I. No government is known to recognise it.

avram.story:
The Grand Duchy of Avram is a micronation in Tasmania, Australia, that claims no land and works mainly as a private bank issuing its own money. John Charlton Rudge, a former Liberal Party member of the Tasmanian parliament, started it in the early 1980s and calls it "philosophical, not territorial". He styles himself Grand Duke and claims dozens of titles. His Royal Bank of Avram opened in shops he owned in George Town and later moved to Strahan.
Customers exchanged Australian dollars for its banknotes and coins, which were linked to the value of gold. Because the bank had no licence, the Australian government seized Rudge's currency reserves and went to the Federal Court. Six cases followed at a cost of about 22 million Australian dollars, the courts found he had done nothing illegal, and they ordered the property returned.
Rudge resumed banking and issued more coins and notes, the most recent dated 2008. The bank's later activity is not known.

sovereign-yidindji-government.story:
The Sovereign Yidindji Government is a government set up by members of the Yidindji, an Aboriginal people of northern Queensland in Australia, who renounced their legal ties with Australia in 2014 (a list of micronations says 2013). Gudju Gudju Gimuybara is chief minister and Murrumu Walubara Yidindji is foreign and trade minister. It claims about 2,500 square kilometres south of Port Douglas, through Cairns and inland across the Atherton Tablelands, plus 80 kilometres of sea.
It issues its own driver's licences. In May 2015 Queensland police charged Murrumu after finding him with a licence and number plates from the Yidindji government, and he argued that the police had no jurisdiction, or legal authority, over him. How the case ended is not known. In 2022 the group launched a digital Sovereign Yidindji Dollar, pegged to the Australian dollar. It hopes for a formal agreement with the Australian government and has approached Russia and Venezuela.
sovereign-yidindji-government.mechanism: Issuing its own licences brought the claim into a traffic court, where Australian law meets the assertion of sovereignty, the right to rule oneself. A claim of this kind is tested when someone acts on it in daily life.

glacier-republic.story:
The Glacier Republic is a mock state that the environmental group Greenpeace declared over Chile's glaciers on 5 March 2014, to push Chile into passing a law protecting them. Greenpeace objected to mining companies building on or near glaciers. It said Chile's law left a legal vacuum, because neither the constitution nor the water code names glaciers as a public good that must be protected, and Chile had no specific glacier law.
It also pointed to unclear points in the border between Chile and Argentina. It took out a full-page advertisement in The New York Times, and more than 40,000 people signed up as citizens within ten days. Greenpeace said the republic would hand the glaciers back to Chile once a suitable law passed. Some Chilean laws may already cover glaciers, including the Civil Code, which makes waters state property, and an environmental law listing glaciers among protected wetlands.
Six deputies introduced a glacier bill in 2014, and it was still being debated in late 2015. Whether a law has since passed is not known.

holy-empire-of-reunion.story:
The Holy Empire of Reunion is an invented country created on 28 August 1997 by law students at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil. It claims Réunion, an island of about 2,511 square kilometres in the Indian Ocean that is an overseas department of France, meaning a full administrative part of the French state. The project has been described as a parody of the French department and as a simulation for practising politics and constitutional law.
A Brazilian newspaper covered it in 1998 when it moved onto the internet. It is not known to have tried to take control of the island or to have drawn any response from France, and whether the project is still active is not known.

federal-republic-of-montmartre-ny.story:
The Most Serene Federal Republic of Montmartre was a mock country claiming Manhattan's Theater District in New York City, from about 39th to 59th Street. Its founder and president was Barry Alan Richmond, a stage actor and director, who proclaimed it around 1965 and said it dated from a French colony founded in 1636. He called it a "political fiction" and part of what he termed "total theater", and he paid for phone listings in the government pages of the Manhattan directory.
New York Telephone wanted the "Montmartre Govt Of" listing removed, and in 1977 the dispute went to the New York Public Service Commission, the state body that regulates utilities. An examiner ruled for the company on 30 June, and the commission set that ruling aside on 7 July. The company still printed 955,000 directories without the listing that August, and Richmond lost a court case to restore it in April 1978.
In December 1979 he announced that the commission had ruled for him. A 2001 article found him still running it, claiming half of Kennedy Airport. Nothing later is known about it.

vikesland.story: The Kingdom of Vikesland was a micronation, a self-declared country that no government recognises, in Brandon, Manitoba, Canada. A television news cameraman founded it in 2005 for a documentary about micronations, and it claimed his home and a property he owned jointly with someone else. It lasted until 2018. No response from the Canadian government is known.

keraton-agung-sejagat.story:
Keraton Agung Sejagat, meaning Universal Grand Throne, was a mystical movement and invented kingdom based in Purworejo Regency, Central Java, Indonesia. Its founders, Totok Santoso Hadiningrat and Dyah Gitarja, began it in 2018 and gathered around 450 members. Hadiningrat said that a ruler of the old Majapahit Empire had handed sovereignty, meaning supreme authority, to the Portuguese in 1518 on condition that it be returned after 500 years.
On that basis he claimed authority over every country on Earth, including the United Nations and the Pentagon. Members paid about 200 dollars each for uniforms and titles. In January 2020 the group held a public ritual in a Purworejo township, and residents who were uneasy about it complained to the police. Police arrested the two founders days later. On 21 January Hadiningrat told a press conference that the kingdom was a scam and its history was made up.
A University of Indonesia historian also pointed out that the Majapahit Empire had collapsed in 1478, before the supposed treaty. How any case against them ended is not known.

principality-of-filettino.story:
Filettino is a village of about 554 people, some 70 kilometres east of Rome in Italy, that announced in 2011 it would become an independent principality. The Italian government had passed an austerity package of about 50 billion euros, which required towns of fewer than 1,000 people to merge with their neighbours. The mayor, Luca Sellari, would have lost his job under the plan, and he wanted the town to keep managing its own land, forests and water.
So he led a campaign to make Filettino a self-governing principality, pointing to the many small states that existed before Italy was unified. The town printed a currency called the fiorito with his picture on it and sold T-shirts with a new coat of arms. Not everyone agreed, and a local restaurant owner said residents wanted to run their own resources but not to leave Italy.
By November 2011 the merger had still not gone ahead, although the government was pressing the town to share services. What became of the principality after that is not known.

puntland.story:
Puntland is a self-governing state in north-east Somalia, on the Horn of Africa, with its capital at Garowe. Somalia's civil war began in 1991, the year its ruler Siad Barre fell. In 1998 local politicians, elders, business people and civil groups held a three-month conference in Garowe, and on 1 August they founded Puntland to provide services, security and trade. It was set up as a homeland for the Harti clan group, with the Majeerteen clan as its chief architects.
It covers 212,510 square kilometres, and its 2016 population estimate was 4,334,633. It has its own constitution, adopted at a convention in April 2012. Unlike Somaliland, its neighbour to the west, which claims to be a separate country, Puntland has held that it is part of Somalia, and it disputes the Sool, Sanaag and Ayn regions with Somaliland. On 31 March 2024, during a dispute over Somalia's constitution, Puntland said it no longer recognised the federal government, would stop taking part in federal institutions, and would exercise the powers of an independent state until a federal constitution is approved in a referendum it takes part in. No foreign government is known to recognise it as a separate state.

liechtenstein-purchase.mechanism: A family bought land from an indebted count with the emperor's approval, and the emperor then raised it to a principality. Land and ruling rights both passed because the emperor agreed, and full independence came in 1806 when the empire was breaking up.

congo-free-state.mechanism: A private person turned bundles of treaties with local leaders into a state by persuading outside powers to recognise it, meaning to accept it as a state. One account from the time says the local leaders who signed did not understand a word of the treaties.

lundy-harman.mechanism: Buying an island brings ownership of the land, and national law still applies there. Harman's conviction showed that a private owner cannot issue money in a place that remains part of the state.

niihau-robinson.mechanism: A monarch sold the land, and the family has kept it through the change from kingdom to United States rule. Ownership gives the family the power to control who enters, but no separate right to rule the island.

liberia-cape-mesurado.mechanism: A private society obtained land from a local ruler and governed it as a colony, and the settlers later declared a state. The colony expanded at times by force against the people already living there.

golden-triangle-kings-romans.mechanism: A lease of this kind leaves the land in Laos while giving a company wide control of what happens there. Laos keeps the legal right to rule, though the place operates much like a separate Chinese-speaking territory.

ras-el-hekma.mechanism: The buyer acquired development rights over land in Egypt, and Egypt kept a share of the project. The announcement describes an investment and does not mention handing over the right to rule the land.

bolivian-syndicate-acre.mechanism: A state tried to hold a remote region by leasing it to foreign investors with powers close to a government's. Neighbouring states refused to accept this, and the company was bought out when the region passed to Brazil by treaty.

liberland.mechanism: A difference between two countries' border claims does not make land free to take, because the country that physically controls it can treat anyone entering as an illegal border crosser, whatever documents they hold.

kingitanga.mechanism: Māori chiefs set up their own monarchy in opposition to colonial rule. The colonial government took much of the movement's land by force and confiscation, but the monarchy continues, with no standing in New Zealand law.

akhzivland.mechanism: A long-tolerated occupant can stay on through a personal stand-off with a state and even win a lease. The lease is an ordinary contract under Israeli law and gives no right to rule the land.

atlantium.mechanism: Buying land gave the group a base, but the land stayed under Australian law, so owning the property did not make it a country.

goust.mechanism: Being described as independent did not make Goust independent. Its residents went on paying tax to French local government, which shows the state was in charge throughout.

free-republic-of-verdis.mechanism: Croatia physically controls the river bank, and that decides who may stay there, whatever documents a claimant holds. Liberland met the same result on a larger scale.

bogota-declaration.mechanism: The Outer Space Treaty bans countries from claiming space but does not say where space begins. Equatorial countries tried to use this omission to claim the orbit above them, and other countries refused, which left the treaty's ban in place.

celestia.mechanism: A county deed office recorded the paper, but a local clerk's registration has no effect on who holds the right to rule anything.

ms-the-world.mechanism: People can live permanently at sea without claiming any country of their own by using an ordinary flag registration. The flag state, the country where the ship is registered, supplies the law on board.

hawaiian-sovereignty-movement.mechanism: A government's apology for an illegal act does not by itself restore sovereignty, the right of a people to rule themselves, or return land. Any change would need new law or a new negotiation.

ganienkeh.mechanism: Negotiation with New York State produced a lease and left open whether the group had any right to rule itself. Courts have since ruled against the trust over back taxes, which shows the state's law still reaches the land.

laas-en-bearn.mechanism: A village council can call itself a principality as protest and publicity. Its legal basis is an ordinary association under French law, and France's right to rule the village is unaffected.

johnson-v-mintosh.mechanism: Private citizens could not buy land from Native American nations, because only the sovereign, the government with the right to rule, could acquire it. The rule made the state the only lawful buyer, whatever price or agreement a private person might reach.

herzl-palestine-offer.mechanism: Part of a state can be sold only if its ruler agrees, and the sultan refused even while in debt. Herzl's later plan offered debt relief as the price and asked for autonomy, or limited self-rule, instead of full control.

aisland-landi.mechanism: Landi hoped distance from land would keep him beyond extradition. Living at sea also raises the question of who checks a barge's safety, and neither a flag state (the country whose rules a vessel sails under) nor an inspection body has been named.
